The figure on the bridge turns its thrown-forward shadow toward the window, the way a man turns toward a draught he didn't know was open, and Itsuki makes a sound you have never heard him make. You break the contact the only way you can, with your whole body, and when it's done he is sitting on the studio floor and the canvas on the easel is blank — scraped clean by nothing you did, the overpass gone, the figure gone, the month of work gone — and when he reaches for it his fingers find the surface and no colour will come.

choices.x: Go to him first. The trail can hold for a breath.
choices.hint: Choose the friend over the lead. Gin is still north and still going; the seconds you spend on the studio floor are seconds the tide takes back — but Itsuki, white and shaking and unable to find his own colour, is the cost of this road made flesh, and he is in front of you now.

choices.x: Fix the heading first, while the sight is fresh.
choices.hint: Pin down exactly where the window showed Gin before the image fades. You'll lose nothing of the trail and a little of yourself — Itsuki will tell you he's fine, and you will choose, this once, to be told.

choices.x: Ask him what he saw that you couldn't.
choices.hint: His sight is older than yours and reads layers you only felt. He saw something in the tide he hasn't said — and prying it out of a man who just lost his colour for you is a thing you will have to decide whether you are.

beats.scene: What you owe, and to whom
prose: You come back to the morning owing a debt with no number on it, and Itsuki owing the house more, and the city sitting a half-degree off true from the places you have stood tonight where no one should stand. The Kuroda have what they wanted, which was your measure; you have what you came for, which is worse and better than a location — you have the seam, the tide, the proof that your brother is still in there and the timing that says not for long. The Towers will not follow a seated Duty. You will. That gap, between what the oldest house in Tokyo has decided it cannot afford and what you cannot afford not to do, is the whole shape of the road you have just walked, and it points north, toward water, the way every road on this morning eventually does.

Itsuki gets up off the floor, because he is the kind of man who gets up, and he turns the blank canvas back to the wall the way you turn a photograph of someone you are not ready to have died. It'll come back, he says, of the colour, and you both let it be true in the room even though neither of you knows it. He does not ask you what you'll do with what he spent to show you. He has known you fifteen years; he already knows you'll spend it, all of it, the way you spend everything, on Gin. The not-asking is the most he will let himself say, and you hear all of it.

What you carry out of the studio into Book Two is the family's cold cosmology and one warm, ruinous reading laid over it: that the thing wearing your brother has a seat to claim and a wall to thin and a perfectly reasonable case, and that the man under it is awake enough to be afraid and not free enough to run. The lanterns are guttering along the Nezu lane as you leave — the small fires the Kuroda lit for nothing, hung for no returning dead — and you understand, with the half-degree of new wrongness the night has put in you, exactly why a house that old declines to invite anything back across a membrane it has spent its whole existence learning not to thin.

choices.x: North, now, on the heading the sight gave you.
choices.hint: Carry the road straight into the Handwriting and go after Gin while the tide still leaves enough of him to reach. You go with the seam in your eyes and a friend behind you who cannot paint.

choices.x: Make the repayment to Itsuki first, whatever it costs you.
choices.hint: Refuse to leave the studio owing the one debt that was never the house's. There is no currency for it and you go looking anyway — which is either the most honest thing you do all night or the slowest.

choices.x: Keep the Kuroda's silence — and start counting what it will cost you later.
choices.hint: Honour the trade you made with the cousin and feel the collar of it settle. The lower houses, the Grid, the CVD: every road after this one is harder for the word you have promised never to say.

cvd.title: The Directorate
acts: Open: become theirs to be allowed in
Deepen: the briefing Gin skipped, from the inside
Converge: the file that should not exist

beats.scene: CVD intake, Kasumigaseki, before the desks fill
prose: The Civil Veil Directorate does not look like a place that crosses to the dead. It looks like every other ministry annex in Kasumigaseki at this hour — fluorescent strip light over grey carpet tile, a vending machine humming to no one, a wall clock that has been forty seconds slow for so long that the staff have stopped trusting it. You came here because every other door you tried this morning gave you a brother-shaped silence, and the one institution that should have logged Gin missing has logged nothing at all. That nothing is the loudest thing in Tokyo right now, and the only way to read it is from inside.

Registration is not a form. It is a small white room and a woman named Okada Shizuka who does not ask your name because she has known it, you slowly realize, for four years. She slides a single laminated card across the table — the Postulate, they call it, the test that decides whether the city files you as a citizen who saw something or a medium who is something — and she watches your hands more than your face while you read it. Most people lie on this without meaning to, she says, not unkindly. The veil doesn't care what you wish were true. Neither do we. Behind her, Obon decorations someone hung without conviction sag in the air-conditioning: paper lanterns for the returning dead, in the one building in the country that knows exactly how literally to take them.

You understand, holding the card, that this is the first door and that it only opens one way. To present cleanly — to let them read you, name you, file you — is to hand the Directorate a key to the part of yourself you have spent your whole life keeping two locks ahead of everyone. But the alternative is to stay outside, where Gin's absence is a private grief instead of an institutional fact, and grief has never once told you where someone went.

choices.x: Present clean. Let the Postulate read you true.
choices.hint: They will know exactly what you are by lunchtime — both registers, the searching, all of it. A medium files faster than a citizen. So does a liability.

choices.x: Present as a witness, not a medium. Hold one register back.
choices.hint: Slower clearance, smaller access — but they file you as ordinary, and the part of you that frightens you stays yours. Gin's trail is behind doors a witness never reaches.

choices.x: Ask Okada why she already knows your name.
choices.hint: She will tell you, and what she tells you will mean your brother prepared this room for you years ago — which means he knew, years ago, that you would one day need it.

beats.scene: Director Adachi's office, two floors above the carpet tile
prose: Director Adachi keeps his office colder than the rest of the building and his voice warmer, and you spend the first minute trying to decide which one is the lie. He has your file open — thin, suspiciously thin for a man who registered an hour ago — and he reads from it the way a doctor reads a chart he has already memorized, for your benefit, to let you feel consulted. Uedera's brother, he says, and lets the surname sit in the cold air between you. He spoke of you. Not often. Once, properly. He does not say when. You will spend weeks deciding the when mattered.

What Adachi offers is real and the catch is also real, and he is too good at this to pretend otherwise. Clearance, casework, the ladder — the Directorate will let you climb toward the floors where your brother's name still lives in active systems, but every rung is a thing the institution does to you in exchange. You will carry their flag to scenes. You will file what you find in the shape they prefer it filed. And somewhere above this office, in rooms Adachi gestures at without looking, are the five families who decide which of the Directorate's truths survive contact with their interests. I am the ceiling you can see, he tells you, almost gently. I'd rather you knew that now than discovered it at a worse hour.

Okada is in the room and says nothing, which you are learning is how she says the most. When Adachi steps out to take a call he was always going to take, she leans in and gives you the only thing she has been waiting four years to give: that Gin's last instruction to her, the one he left like a stone in a riverbed for the current to uncover, was not protect the Directorate and not find me. It was when my brother comes, do not let them assess him on a Thursday. She does not know why. You are starting to.

choices.x: Take the ladder. Climb toward Gin's name, on their terms.
choices.hint: Access opens fast. So does the slow conversion of you into the institution's instrument — by the time you reach his floor you may be the kind of person who would file him away.

choices.x: Take only enough clearance to work cases, refuse the climb.
choices.hint: Stay small enough that the families never notice you. You also stay small enough that the doors with your brother behind them stay shut a great deal longer.

choices.x: Ask Okada what happens on Thursdays.
choices.hint: She will tell you it is assessment day, when the Auditors read mediums down to the registers — and that something about you, read on a Thursday, is what Gin spent his last free act trying to prevent.

beats.scene: First clearance, first call-out, Kita-ku after dark
prose: Your first scene is a fourth-floor walk-up in Kita where a woman has been hearing her late husband run the bath at 3:47 every morning, and you are not the lead. The lead is Nakamura Aoi, junior like you but a year deeper, and she works a haunting the way other people defuse something — slowly, with her whole attention, narrating nothing she does not have to. She clocks your registers the instant the cold front of the apartment touches you, you can see her clock it, and the only thing she says is breathe out before you reach, not in, which is the first useful thing anyone in this building has ever told you about what you are.

Kato Ryusei takes the report, because Kato takes every report, and his eyes do the small soft thing they do when Aoi speaks that he has not yet noticed they do. The case itself is ordinary in the worst way — a man who died with one unfinished motion and a wife who cannot stop hearing him try to complete it — and you watch Aoi cross just far enough to tell him the bath is run, it has been run, he can stop, and then come back with her hands shaking and her face perfectly still. That's the job, she says afterward on the stairwell, not looking at you. You go where they're stuck and you tell them it's done. The trick is believing it on the way back.

It is on those stairs, with the lantern-smell of Obon coming up the well from someone's open window, that Aoi mentions Gin without knowing she is handing you a knife. She worked one rotation under him. She noticed when he stopped coming in. And the thing that has bothered her since — the thing she has not filed because there is no field on the form for it — is that the absence is the wrong shape. A man who quits leaves a quitting-shaped hole. Gin left something else. She does not have the word. You do, and you do not say it, because to say it on a stairwell at Obon to a near-stranger is to make it true.

choices.x: Tell Aoi the word. Trust her with the shape.
choices.hint: She is the first person in the building who saw it too. Trust bought this early is real — and it makes her a person the institution can now hurt to get to you.

choices.x: Say nothing. Let her keep the question.
choices.hint: Protect her by leaving her with a mystery instead of a target. You also walk the rest of this road one ally lighter, carrying the shape alone.

choices.x: Ask her what Gin was working when the shape changed.
choices.hint: She will give you a date and a district — Kita, the low places near the water — and a date is a thread, and threads in this building are how the families find out you are pulling.

beats.scene: The briefing archive, the Thursday that has a hole in it
prose: Every briefing the Directorate runs is logged, transcribed, and shelved, which means somewhere in this building is the record of the last briefing your brother attended and the record of the first one in nine years that he did not. You requisition them both. The clearance you spent to do it costs you a favour you will not understand the price of until later, but the woman at the records cage stamps the slip without reading it, because at this hour even the Directorate runs on people too tired to ask why.

The attended briefings read like a man at the top of his craft — Gin's questions in the margins, sharp, three moves ahead of the room, the handwriting you would know in the dark. And then the Thursday. The transcript exists; the seat does not. There is a gap in the round-table log shaped exactly like a Vanguard who was expected and did not come, and the remarkable thing, the thing that lifts the hair on your arms in the over-lit cage, is that no one chased it. A man who has not missed a Thursday in nine years skips one and the system simply closes around the space — a sign-off here, a reassignment there, a note in a hand you do not recognize saying the matter was handled at a level above the room. Handled, in this building, you are learning, is a verb that means buried with permission.

You read the after-action on the case that briefing was meant to cover, and it is the wrong kind of clean. A drowning in the Kita lowlands, the low place where the water remembers, closed in under two days with a confidence the evidence does not earn. Whoever signed it wanted it gone. And tucked in the appendix, a body-reading you were not cleared to see, initialled by a specialist named Kurosawa — three lines, then redaction, then the only words that survived the black bar: double-layer. not consistent with the registered subject. recommend escalation. The escalation never happened. Someone above the room decided your brother's body was a sentence best left unfinished.

choices.x: Find Kurosawa. Ask what 'double-layer' means.
choices.hint: He read your brother and lived to redact it. He can tell you what is wearing Gin — but a specialist who talks twice is a specialist Internal Affairs starts watching, and so are his visitors.

choices.x: Pull the thread on who signed the Thursday away.
choices.hint: The signature leads up, toward the families and the floors Adachi only gestured at. Follow it and you stop being a junior reading files and start being a problem with a name.

choices.x: Copy the redacted reading and tell no one yet.
choices.hint: Evidence in your pocket is leverage and liability in one envelope. The Directorate has rooms for people who walk out with what they were not cleared to keep.

beats.scene: Kurosawa's lab, where the bodies are read and not believed
prose: Kurosawa works in a sub-level the building pretends is storage, and he reads bodies the way a restorer reads a painting that has been painted over — looking for the under-image, the thing the surface was put there to hide. He is not surprised you found him. He has been waiting, in the specific way of a man who did the right thing once, filed it, watched it vanish, and has been living since inside the question of whether he should have shouted instead. When you say the word double-layer he stops pretending to work.

What he tells you, carefully, with the door watched, is the physiology of a haunting that is not a haunting. Possession in the Directorate's textbooks is a fever — a thing that rides hot and clumsy and burns its host out in weeks. What he read in Gin was the opposite: cold, patient, tidy, a second register laid down under the first as deliberately as a second coat of paint, a presence that was not consuming the host but preserving him, keeping him functional, keeping him filing, keeping him at his desk nine days a week. I have read a great many possessed, Kurosawa says. I have never read one being taken care of. Whatever is in your brother does not want him dead. It wants him working.

He gives you the name of the only operational fact that survived the cover-up — a clerk named Tanaka, who sits behind Kurosawa in the org chart and in front of him in the chain that buried the reading, and who knows the single concrete thing the redaction was built to hide: not what Gin is, but where the recommendation went when escalation was denied. A name on a routing slip. A floor. I read the symptom, Kurosawa says, already turning back to his work, already rehearsing his innocence. Tanaka can tell you who decided the symptom was convenient. After that you are on your own, and so, I'm afraid, is your brother.

choices.x: Go to Tanaka straight, before the building closes around it.
choices.hint: Speed beats the cover-up, but a junior who sprints from Kurosawa's lab to a routing clerk draws a line on a map that Internal Affairs can read as easily as you can.

choices.x: Bring it to Moriya in Internal Affairs first.
choices.hint: IA is the one body that can subpoena up past Adachi — or the one body that can make a discrepancy, and the person carrying it, both quietly disappear. You will not know which Moriya is until you are inside the room.

choices.x: Sit with what Kurosawa said: it wants Gin working. Ask why.
choices.hint: The answer reframes everything — a demon that preserves its host is a demon with a project — but following the thought means admitting your brother is not a victim being drained, he is a tool being maintained, and toward what you do not yet dare to guess.

beats.scene: Katagiri Noa, and the months that were never filed
prose: Noa agrees to meet you because you are his brother and refuses to meet you anywhere with a Directorate camera, which tells you most of what the conversation will be before it starts. She loved Gin — two years adjacent, the kind of love that is mostly proximity and unspoken timing and one missed window — and she carried something of his for the last months that she never put in a single report, because the form would have made it evidence and she did not want him to be evidence yet. Across a café table in Nippori, with the Obon crowds thick outside and the lanterns going up along the shōtengai, she finally makes him evidence, for you.

He changed, she says, not all at once. The work got better and the man got worse — sharper case-closure rates and a new, terrible patience, as if someone had taken her colleague and ironed him flat. He started talking about duty the way the devout talk about grace, an interrupted duty, a thing left undischarged, and once, late, after a closing they should have celebrated, he had looked at the Kita lowlands across the water and said a sentence she has not been able to set down since: The wall is thinner there than the maps admit, and somebody has to decide whether thin is the same as wrong. She thought it was exhaustion. She is telling you now because she has finally understood it was a plan, said out loud, by something using his mouth and his exhaustion as cover.

Then she gives you the thing she has been protecting, the unfiled truth that is also the kindest and cruelest fact you will carry out of this road: that in his last lucid month, Gin came to her once, briefly, all the way himself — she could tell, she will always be able to tell — and asked her to make sure that if anyone ever came looking, they understood he had not chosen this and could not, now, choose out of it alone. He didn't ask me to save him, Noa says, and does not cry, which is worse. He asked me to make sure someone knew the difference between him and the thing wearing him. I think he meant you.

choices.x: Promise Noa you'll hold the difference, whatever it costs.
choices.hint: It is the right promise and the one you cannot fully keep — the deeper you go, the harder it gets to tell the brother from the thing, and a promise like this can become the rope you hang on.

choices.x: Ask for everything she remembers about the Kita lowlands.
choices.hint: She has been to the low place with him. What she remembers is a map no file holds — and walking it means walking toward the exact wall your brother's borrower wants thinned.

choices.x: Ask whether she'd testify, if it came to Internal Affairs.
choices.hint: Her word could break the cover-up open. It would also put the woman who loved your brother in front of the families' machinery, and she has already lost him once.

beats.scene: Public Confidence, where files are kept clean by being emptied
prose: Hagiwara Mizuki runs the office the Directorate does not advertise, the one called Public Confidence, whose job is not to lie to the city but to decide which truths the city can survive knowing — and she summons you, which means you have become a truth she is now weighing. Her office is the warmest room in the building and the most dangerous, full of soft light and good tea and the unhurried manner of a person who has erased better-credentialed people than you before the second cup. She knows about the requisition. The Kurosawa copy. The visit to Noa. She lays your last week out on the table like a hand of cards she has already won, and then she does the thing that nearly works: she is reasonable.

There is an address, she explains, that does not exist. A case closed too fast, a body-reading that recommends an escalation the institution chose not to survive, a Vanguard whose absence was handled above the room — and all of it, she says, is true, and all of it, she says, is also a wall holding back a flood you cannot see the size of. The five families did not bury your brother out of cruelty, she tells you, refilling your cup. They buried him because the alternative was a panic this city is not built to hold. You can have the truth or you can have the city standing the morning after. I have spent my career learning you almost never get both. She offers you the address. She offers you a future in the Directorate. The price is that you take the second in exchange for never speaking the first.

And here is the trap, the elegant centre of it: she is not entirely wrong. Some part of what she says is the most honest thing anyone in this building has told you. The membrane in the Kita lowlands is thinning, the panic would be real, and a younger, frightened version of you would take the deal and call it maturity. But you have read the under-image now. You know the thing wearing your brother is not a flood the families are containing — it is a project they have decided is cheaper to permit than to fight, and Mizuki's reasonable, grieving city is the alibi a thinned wall hides behind. The clean file she is offering you is not a kindness. It is the last door, and it only opens one way.

choices.x: Take the address. Trade your silence for the door.
choices.hint: You reach the place no file admits — and you arrive as the institution's instrument, having already practiced, once, the act of filing a truth away. The first time is the hardest. She is counting on there being a second.

choices.x: Refuse, and walk out carrying everything you've found.
choices.hint: You keep your mouth and lose the door, the ladder, and the protection. The families do not forgive a junior who chooses the flood over the wall, and you have just told the warmest room in the building exactly what you are.

choices.x: Pretend to take the deal. Let her think the wall held.
choices.hint: Buy the address with a lie and walk out still yourself — but Mizuki erases better liars than you for a living, and a deal you intend to break is a debt that comes due at the worst possible hour.

beats.scene: The file that should not exist, read at last by its own light
prose: However you came by it — bought, stolen, or refused into your hands by accident — the address that no file admits is real, and it is in the Kita lowlands, the low place where the water remembers, the wall your brother said was thinner than the maps allow. You stand in the records cage one last time with the institution's own paper in your hands and you understand, finally, what the Directorate was for in this road: not to hide your brother from you, but to teach you to read the way he learned to read, in the demanded order, one buried node at a time, until the shape underneath the shape stands up off the page and looks back.

Because it is all here, in the cleanest filing in Tokyo. The skipped briefing was not Gin avoiding his duty; it was the borrower keeping the host away from a room where a sharp colleague might have read the cold under his skin. The case closed too fast was the lowland drowning — a soul that crossed too easily, through a wall already going thin, evidence the project was working. The body-reading buried above the room was the truth filed where the truth goes to be convenient. And the five families' reasonable, grieving silence is the permission a Duty-register demon needed to keep your brother at his desk, productive, preserved, plotting the thinning of the Kita membrane behind nine years of perfect attendance and a single, deliberate, telling absence.

You leave the Directorate the way you came, through the lobby and the sagging Obon lanterns and the wall clock that is still forty seconds slow, and nothing about you looks different to the tired people at the desks. But you are carrying the institution's own hand back to the Handwriting now — the dates, the routing slip, the word double-layer, the name Yushiro you have not yet let yourself say aloud — and for the first time since the cold kitchen and the 3:47 that started all of this, you are not chasing a brother-shaped silence. You are reading the thing that made the silence, in its own ledger, in the order it demanded, toward the wall it wants thinned. The Directorate gave you the only honest gift it had: it taught you to see the project. What you do with the seeing belongs to the books that come after.

choices.x: Take the file to the Kita lowlands. Read the wall yourself.
choices.hint: The next truth is at the thinning place, not in any cage. But the borrower wanted you reading paper, not standing at the membrane — arrive there and you arrive where the project can see you back.

choices.x: Carry it back to the Handwriting. Cross-read it against Gin's own nodes.
choices.hint: His Archive and the Directorate's file are the same map drawn by enemy hands. Laid together they name Yushiro — and naming it is the moment the searching ends and the harder thing begins.

choices.x: Burn your copy. Keep only what you can carry in your head.
choices.hint: Paper can be subpoenaed, planted, or used to bury you the way it buried the reading. Memory can't be requisitioned — but memory is also the one record the thing wearing your brother already knows how to edit.

grid.title: The Grid
acts: Converge: contraband, and the only honest tool in the city

beats.scene: Gin's apartment, the back pages of a book that is not a notebook
prose: You go back to the apartment because the official roads all ask you to start by handing your brother's name to someone, and you are not ready to do that yet. The kettle is still cold. On the shelf where Gin kept the things he did not file is a paperback with the spine broken white — a train timetable from a line that stopped running in 2003, the kind of thing he collected and you never asked about — and when you fan it the pencil is there in the margins, small, cramped, in his own hand, names that are not names so much as the city's quiet directions to a person: the woman who reads cats, Sugamo, ask for the litter not the medium. The boy at the noodle stand under the tracks who knows when a place has gone wrong before it shows. The old courier — only ever the old courier.

These are the people the Directorate's files cannot see, because the Directorate's files are a map of everyone who agreed to be on a map. Gin worked the registered city by day and wrote this other one down by night, the unregistered web of mediums and sensitives and small ugly miracles that the CVD would shut in a cell if it could be bothered to believe in them. He kept it for the cases the official channel closed too fast — and you understand, holding the timetable, that your brother trusted these margins with things he did not trust to his own colleagues. That he wrote them small so that no one reading over his shoulder would know what they were worth.

There is a number under the last name, no area code, the kind you dial from a payphone or not at all. To call it is to walk into Gin's other life through the back door, wearing his face — the two of you were always taken for each other in low light — and to ask the people who keep no records to do the one thing they exist to do: find someone the records have lost. It is also to tell a network that survives on never being looked at that a CVD-adjacent stranger is now looking.

choices.x: Call the old courier first — Gin's own last entry.
choices.hint: Start where your brother stopped. The oldest node in the web is the safest to trust and the most dangerous to lose; if he has already gone quiet, you will be walking the one road Gin himself could not finish.

choices.x: Start small — the woman who reads cats, in daylight, in Sugamo.
choices.hint: Ease in through the softest door so the Grid meets you gently. Slow is a luxury, and Gin's lucid windows are closing on a clock you can't see from here.

choices.x: Go to the noodle stand and let yourself be recognised as Gin's face.
choices.hint: Trade on the resemblance to skip the vetting. Wearing your brother's face into rooms that loved him will get you trusted fast — and will cost you the moment they see you are not him.

beats.scene: Sugamo, an upstairs room that smells of cat and cheap incense
prose: The woman who reads cats is younger than the entry made her sound and she does not look at you when you come up the stairs; she looks at the three animals draped along the windowsill, and watches what they do, and reads you off them the way other people read a face. You move like him, she says, meaning Gin, and the grey one on the end stops washing its paw and turns its flat gold attention on you, and she goes very still. But you're lit. He never carried a light into this room. You're one of the ones the wall thins around. She means your sight, the thing you have spent your whole life pretending is nerves. The Grid has no instruments, no clearance levels, no Directorate machines that go ping. It has rooms like this one, and people who notice, and a rule older than the CVD: nobody is owed a reading, and nobody is owed a name.

She tells you the web is awake and afraid, which it is not, usually, in August — Obon is their busy season, the one week the dead are politely expected and the readings come easy. This year the easy readings have gone wrong all across the north of the city. Mediums who could always raise a grandmother are getting a wrongness on the line instead, a pressure, a sense of something standing behind the dead and using them like a curtain. Three of her cats will not go near the north window. She does not know the word for what is happening but you do, because you have read the case the Directorate closed, and the word is membrane, and the place is Kita-ku, and the thing standing behind the curtain is wearing your brother.

She will help you, she says, but the Grid moves by exchange — never money, money leaves a trail — and what she wants is for you to tell her, honestly, with the light you carry, whether the wrongness in the north is going to reach her street. You could read the room for her right now and know. You could also feel the veil flex when you do it, the small cost you have spent your life refusing to pay, the Madness pressing one finger against the inside of your skull and the certainty that somewhere a Directorate sensor just twitched at a use of the Gift it has no file for.

choices.x: Read the room for her — pay the cost, earn the network's trust.
choices.hint: Use the sight openly and the Grid will open to you fast, because you'll have proved you're one of them. Every use thins the veil you're trying to save and tells the watchers exactly what you are.

choices.x: Refuse the reading; offer her Gin's margins instead.
choices.hint: Trade information for information and keep the Gift sheathed. The web trusts the gifted more than the informed; you'll get in, but as a clerk, not as kin.

choices.x: Lie — tell her the north won't reach her, to keep her calm and helpful.
choices.hint: Buy easy cooperation with a comfort you can't back. The Grid's whole economy is honesty between people the state lies to; if the wrongness reaches Sugamo, she will know exactly who told her it wouldn't.

beats.scene: Under the tracks at Ōji, the noodle stand at the hour it stops being open
prose: The boy at the noodle stand is not a boy — the margin lied, or Gin meant something else by the word — he is somewhere past sixty with a young man's hands, and he has been ladling broth at the seam of Kita-ku for thirty years because, he tells you plainly, someone has to stand at a bad place and be ordinary at it. He knows you are coming before you reach the curtain. He has Gin's bowl already set out, the chipped one, and when you do not sit in front of it the way Gin would have he simply moves it aside and pours you your own. So he's gone in, he says, not unkindly. I told him the north was a one-way week. He went anyway. You'll go too. I can see that's already decided.

This, he explains, is what the Grid actually is, under the cat-readers and the brokers and the small ugly miracles: it is the people who live on the seams the official city paved over and pretends are flat. The overpass above you is concrete that has not been right since 2011 and everyone steps across it without naming why. The Directorate has machines that read the veil from offices in Kasumigaseki; the Grid has a man who has stood under the same overpass for thirty years and can tell you to the hour when it has gotten worse. Tonight it has gotten worse. The dead are coming up wrong all along the line, and there is a courier — the old courier, only ever the old courier — who carries the one thing in this city that can tell an honest demon from a borrowed face, and who was due through here two nights ago, and who did not come.

He gives you the broth and the bad news in the same breath, the way people do at seams. The courier's route runs north into exactly the streets the cats won't face. To follow it is to go where the membrane is thinnest, carrying a light, with a Gift that gets louder the closer you get to the thing that wants the wall thin. The boy watches you understand this. Eat first, he says. Whatever you decide. The north doesn't feed you and the dead up there will try to.

choices.x: "Tell me the courier's route. I'll walk it tonight."
choices.hint: Take the thread straight into the thin streets while it's still warm. Two nights cold is already long for a courier; every hour you eat and plan is an hour the membrane is given.

choices.x: "Who else knows the route? I want it from more than one mouth."
choices.hint: Corroborate before you commit, the careful way. Asking around a network that survives by not being asked about will mark you as someone collecting names — and someone, somewhere, is collecting names too.

choices.x: "What was the courier carrying? Say it plainly."
choices.hint: Reach for the prize before the path. Naming the contraband instrument aloud, at a seam, under a thin wall, is exactly the kind of honesty the Grid loves and the listening thing has learned to wait for.

beats.scene: The route north, a map drawn in landmarks no map admits to
prose: There is no address for where the courier goes, only a sequence of seams: the overpass, the shrine that stopped answering, the block of company housing emptied after the relocations, the riverside lot where the water comes up brown and the official gauge has read normal for five years. You walk it in the dark with the boy's directions folded into the shape of your hand, and at each seam the city does the thing seams do — it goes quiet a half-second before you arrive, as though the place had been saying something and stopped when it heard you. Your sight, which you have kept sheathed since Sugamo, will not stay sheathed here. The thin places reach up and read you, and every reading you refuse to give them they take anyway, a little, off the top.

At the shrine that stopped answering you find the first sign of the courier: a tag, the paper kind pilgrims tie to a rack, but tied low and tight in a knot the Grid uses for came through, kept going, and the ink is two days dry. The courier was here. The courier was, by the knot, unhurt and unhunted this far. Past the shrine the knots stop. You stand at the edge of the emptied housing block where the official records closed a hundred families years ago and a single old man still sets a dish of water on a windowsill for a wife the city has declared a closed file, and you feel the membrane here the way you feel a held breath in a room — present, deliberate, thin on purpose. None of these people know they live at the seam. None of them chose to be the place a demon decided the wall was already weak enough to be worth finishing.

Your Gift tells you two things at once and you cannot have both true. It tells you the courier went into the block. It tells you something in the block is using the dead as a curtain, and has been, and is doing it now, and would very much like one more honest gifted person to walk in carrying a light. The old man at the window lifts his dish and nods to you, mistaking you, in the dark, for a son. Behind him the water in the dish is trembling and there is no wind.

choices.x: Go into the block after the courier.
choices.hint: Follow the thread into the thinnest room in the city. The courier may be alive in there; so may the reason the courier stopped tying knots.

choices.x: Stop and read the block from the edge — find the courier before you enter.
choices.hint: Spend the Gift to map the danger first. A full reading this close to the membrane is the loudest thing you could possibly do, and the thing inside has been waiting for exactly that volume.

choices.x: Speak to the old man at the window first.
choices.hint: Trade the courier's lead for a living witness who has watched this seam from the inside for years. He is the most fragile thread here, and pulling on him may be the kindest or the cruellest thing you do tonight.

beats.scene: Inside the block, where the dead are a curtain and someone is holding it
prose: The stairwell of the emptied block holds Obon the way a closed throat holds a word. There are offerings on the landings — fruit gone to glass, water gone to skin — left by no one, because no one lives here, renewed anyway. The dead are present the way the woman in Sugamo warned, thick and polite and wrong, a grandmother's warmth with a pressure behind it, and you understand at last what she meant by a curtain: the dead are real and they are being held up in front of something, the way a hand holds a sheet in front of a thing it does not want seen until the last instant. You climb toward the only door with light under it. Your sight is screaming now, no longer a finger on the skull but a flat palm pressing, and you know that to open that door with the Gift this loud is to be read all the way down by whatever has been borrowing the dead.

The courier is in the room. Alive — and that is the first mercy and the last one. An old woman, smaller than the legend, sitting very upright in a chair that is not hers in an apartment that is not anyone's, with a satchel on her knees that she has not let go of in two days, and her eyes track you in and her mouth says, in your brother's cadence, in a register that is not hers: You came the way he said you would. He does like to be right, your Gin. Even now. Especially now. It is Yushiro. It has not left Kita-ku to be here; it does not need to. The membrane is thin enough now that the Healer can reach through it and wear a mouth at the seam the way it wears your brother at the centre, and it has been sitting in this old woman keeping her alive and afraid for two days specifically so that the thread would lead you in.

The satchel holds the thing the whole Grid is whispering about, and Yushiro knows you know it, and that is the trap's hinge: it does not stop you from taking the contraband instrument. It wants you to take it, because the instrument reads a demon honestly, and an honest reading of Gin is exactly the wound the Healer is counting on to make you choose wrong later — to make you see, in true sight, how little of your brother is left, and despair, and do the merciful, ruinous thing. The courier's hands are white on the strap. Through the borrowed mouth Yushiro says, gently, the Healer's gentleness, the worst thing in the room: Take it. I'm not stopping you. I only ever give people what they ask for.

choices.x: Take the satchel and get the courier out — both, now, before it changes its mind.
choices.hint: Seize the instrument and the witness in one motion. Yushiro is letting you; accepting a gift from the Healer is never free, and you won't see the price until the room you spend it in.

choices.x: Refuse the instrument. Take only the courier.
choices.hint: Deny the demon the wound it's offering and walk out with the living woman instead of the contraband. The Grid will not forgive losing the one honest tool in the city, and you may need exactly what you're leaving on that chair.

choices.x: Make it talk — ask what Gin asked for, in the kitchen, the night it took him.
choices.hint: Stand in the thinnest room in Tokyo and bargain with the thing wearing two mouths at once. Every question you ask, it answers honestly, because the truth from the Healer is the sharpest blade it owns.

beats.scene: The riverside lot, the Directorate's headlights, and a body the water hasn't given up
prose: You come out of the block with the courier on your arm and the night has acquired headlights. The CVD has had a sensor twitch — your reading at the seam, or hers, or the membrane's own loud breathing — and they have come the way the Directorate always comes, two unmarked cars and people who say Centre for Veil Defence as though it were an apology they have stopped meaning. They are not here for the demon; they do not believe the demon the way the Grid believes it. They are here because an unregistered gifted person lit up a forbidden part of the city, and because a Grid fixer downriver has been calling them all night about a body the river has not surfaced — a courier's contact, it turns out, drowned at the seam two nights ago, on the night your courier went dark. The fixer wants the body found before the river gives it up on its own terms and on the official record. The Directorate wants the body found because a body is a file and a file is control.

And you are standing between them holding contraband that can read a seated demon — the single instrument in Tokyo that could prove, to the one institution able to act on it, that something is wearing a CVD analyst named Gin and thinning the Kita membrane on purpose. Show it to the Directorate and they will believe you and take it and take you and fold the whole thing into a clearance level you will never see the inside of again; your brother becomes an asset to be managed, the Grid becomes a list of arrests, and the instrument becomes evidence in a drawer. Keep it from them and you keep your brother yours and your road open, and you leave a real institution blind to a real catastrophe out of nothing nobler than not wanting to lose control of it.

The courier's grip finds your sleeve. Whatever you tell them, she breathes, in her own register now, the demon gone back north to its centre, tell it knowing the river keeps its own accounts. They always surface. Everything up here always, eventually, surfaces. The headlights hold. Somewhere under the brown water a courier's contact waits to become either a Grid favour repaid or a Directorate file opened, and the difference is entirely the next thing out of your mouth.

choices.x: Hand the Directorate the body — not the instrument. Trade the drowned for the contraband.
choices.hint: Give the institution a file it can close and keep the one tool that can't be replaced. You spend a dead stranger's dignity to buy your brother's secret another night; the Grid fixer wanted the body found gently, and the Directorate does not do gentle.

choices.x: Show them the instrument. Make the catastrophe official.
choices.hint: Put the honest tool in the only hands big enough to act on Kita — and lose your brother, the Grid, and the road to a clearance level in the same breath. Some walls are too big for one person to hold up alone, and you'll never know if these hands would have held it.

choices.x: Tell them nothing. Walk the courier out through the seam they won't follow you into.
choices.hint: Refuse both the body and the badge and vanish back into the unregistered dark. The Directorate remembers faces it couldn't file, the river keeps its accounts, and you've now made an enemy of the one institution that could have helped — to keep a road only you can walk.

beats.scene: A back room the Grid keeps for the things it cannot hold in the light
prose: They bring you, finally, to the room behind the rooms — not a place so much as a permission, a basement under a shuttered bathhouse where the Grid keeps the instrument when no one is carrying it, and where the people who run the unregistered city without ever calling themselves that gather to decide what a stranger wearing Gin's face is owed. You set the satchel on the table. Inside is a thing that should not exist by any registry's lights: a reading glass ground from a material the CVD banned in the nineties, set in a frame a dead medium balanced by hand, that does the one honest thing the Directorate's machines refuse to do. It does not measure the veil. It looks through a borrowed face and shows you, in true sight, the exact seam where the person ends and the thing wearing them begins.

It is contraband because honesty is contraband, here, in the registered city — because an instrument that can prove a possession can also prove the Directorate has been managing possessions it called something cleaner, and so the glass has been hunted and hidden and carried by old couriers down routes no map admits to for twenty years. The Grid is offering it to you. Not giving — the Grid does not give — offering, on the network's one unbreakable term: that you bring it back, and that you tell them, honestly, with the light you carry, what you see through it when you turn it on your brother. They have lost couriers to this glass. They will not lose it to a man who looks through it once, sees the thing he loves is mostly gone, and walks into the river the way the contact did.

Through the glass, here, in the safe dark, you can see the membrane plan for what it is at last: the Healer thinning Kita not in one wound but in a hundred seams, each a borrowed mouth, each an emptied block, each an old man's dish of trembling water — a city quietly being made thin enough that a thing without a seat could finish a wall and walk through into the Thirteenth's empty chair. The glass shows you the shape of it. It does not show you what to do. That, the oldest voice in the room tells you, is the curse of the only honest tool in the city: it will never once lie to you about how bad it is, and it will never, ever, tell you it can be fixed.

choices.x: Accept the term. Take the glass north and turn it on Gin.
choices.hint: Carry the honest tool to the one face you cannot afford to read honestly. You will finally see exactly how much of your brother remains — and you will have to keep seeing it, every choice after this, with no mercy of doubt left.

choices.x: Leave the glass with the Grid; carry only what you saw tonight.
choices.hint: Refuse to put a true reading of Gin in your own hands, where despair could use it. You keep hope alive by keeping yourself a little blind — and you walk into the Handwriting without the one proof that could turn an institution.

choices.x: Ask the Grid to read Gin themselves, so the truth isn't yours alone to carry.
choices.hint: Share the weight of the honest sight with people who have carried this glass for twenty years. They have buried couriers who looked too long; they may say yes, and they may say that some readings a brother has to take alone.

beats.scene: The seam at dawn, the glass in your hand, the Handwriting waiting
prose: Obon thins toward its last morning and you stand again at the overpass at Ōji where the boy poured you broth, with the only honest tool in the city wrapped in cloth against your chest and the whole unregistered web now aware, in the way a web is aware, that Gin's brother walks the seams and carries a light. Whatever you decided in the basement, the road has done to you what this road does: it has shown you the catastrophe at full size, a hundred quiet wounds in a city that paved over its seams and called itself flat, and it has refused, the whole way, to hand you an institution to put it down for you. There is no clearance level at the end of the Grid. There is only what you can see, and who will help, and the long account the river keeps.

This is where the unregistered road feeds back into the Handwriting — the slow work of learning the shape in your brother before you have to name it. You came down here for a courier and a name and you are leaving with a glass that will, if you let it, read the change in Gin's hand the way nothing in the registered city can: the entries after the 14th, the lucid windows, the precise seam where Gin ends and the Healer's borrowed cadence begins. The Grid gave you the one tool honest enough to date the handwriting. It also gave you the one tool cruel enough to make you certain too early, before certainty has anywhere to go but down.

The boy is at his stand, opening for a day the dead are no longer politely expected. He sees the cloth against your chest and he sees your face, which is your own now and not your brother's, finally, to anyone paying attention. You'll go north with it, he says, the way he says all the things that are already decided. Just remember the glass only tells you what is. It was never going to tell you what to do about it. That part the Directorate can't do for you, and the family can't, and the dead surely can't. That part's been yours since the kettle went cold. He hands you a bowl you do not have time to eat. You take it anyway, because the Grid trades in honesty, and the honest thing is that you are not ready, and you go north regardless.

choices.x: Go north now, glass in hand, and read the Handwriting honestly.
choices.hint: Carry the only honest tool straight into your brother's failing script. You'll know, after this, exactly what's left of Gin — and you can never again pretend, to yourself, that you don't.

choices.x: Go to the other roads first — bring the Grid's truth to the people who can act.
choices.hint: Take what the seams showed you to Itsuki, or the CVD, or your own Gift, and try to build a hand big enough to hold a wall. Every road you walk to is a road the membrane thins while you travel it.

choices.x: Sit down and eat the boy's bowl. Be unready, out loud, for one more minute.
choices.hint: Refuse, briefly, to be the person the seam needs. It changes nothing about the wall and everything about whether you walk north as a brother or as a tool — and the difference is the whole story.

power.title: The Forbidden Reach
acts: Open: read the room, pay the Madness
Deepen: the Directorate notices what you are

beats.scene: The kitchen, 3:47 still on the stove clock, and the decision not to ask anyone
prose: Every other road out of this room begins by handing a name to someone with a badge or a grudge, and you have stood here long enough to understand that you are not going to do that. The factions want your brother's name because a name is a handle, and a handle is how a thing gets carried somewhere you can't follow. You have a different instrument, the one your family spent your whole childhood teaching you to keep folded shut — the two registers behind your eyes that have never once been allowed to open at the same time, the sight your mother called nerves and your aunt called a debt. You can find Gin yourself. You only have to stop pretending you can't.

You put your hand flat on the counter where he was standing when the city ate him, and you let the first fold come undone. It is not dramatic. It is the opposite of dramatic — a small loosening, like a held breath you didn't know was being held, and then the kitchen is suddenly very loud with information that was always here: the cooling shape of where a body stood, the seam in the air at chest height where something passed through that should not be able to pass through anything, the faint pencil-warmth of his hands on the timetable on the shelf. Your sight does not show you pictures. It shows you the cost of looking, and the looking, arriving together, so that you cannot have one without paying for the other.

And underneath all of it, far down, a pressure puts one cool finger against the inside of your skull and waits to see if you'll keep going. This is the thing the family was afraid of. Not the demons, not the Directorate — this. The way the veil thins from your side when you reach hard through it, the way each reach makes the next one easier and the world thinner, until easy and thin are the same word and you are the door instead of the one standing at it. You can find Gin tonight, with your own eyes, paying your own price. The only question is how much you are willing to spend before you've even left the room.

choices.x: Open both registers at once — full sight, here, now.
choices.hint: Unfold everything and the seam will give up Gin's direction in seconds. Your family never let the two registers open together for a reason; the first thing they show you in stereo is the inside of the veil, and it shows you back.

choices.x: Open one register only, and walk the residue out the door behind it.
choices.hint: Half the sight, half the price, twice the time. Slow tracking keeps you human longer, but Gin's lucid windows close on a clock you can't see, and the residue cools by the hour.

choices.x: Fold it shut again and just look — with your eyes, like anyone.
choices.hint: Refuse the Gift entirely and you stay clean, unread, unnoticed. You also stay blind, and every other road from this kitchen ends with you owing a faction the very thing you were trying to protect.

beats.scene: The streets north, after midnight, reading the city like a wound that hasn't closed
prose: Once you are reaching, the city will not stop talking. You walk and the sight overlays the ordinary Obon streets — the paper lanterns, the late ramen steam, the families home for the dead — with a second map drawn in pressure and residue, and on that map your brother is a line of cooling footprints that the rain hasn't been able to wash because they were never quite physical to begin with. You follow them the way you'd follow a smell of smoke, north and north, through Sugamo and toward Kita, and the further you go the more the second map and the first one disagree about what is real. By the third intersection you are stepping over a low wall in the sight-map that the eye-map insists is an open road, and your foot believes the sight.

The Madness is not voices, which is the lie everyone tells about it. It is grammar. The world's small rules — that doors are shut until opened, that the dead are quiet, that a face belongs to one person — begin to feel like suggestions you are free to decline, and the freedom is the danger, because somewhere in the declining is the moment you step off a real platform onto a sight-map train. You catch yourself at the edge of exactly that, one shoe over the yellow line, a real train screaming through where your second map had drawn a corridor, and you stand on the trembling platform afterward shaking, having learned the road's only law in your body: the brighter you reach, the less the world is required to be true around you.

But the footprints are warmer now. He came this way, and recently, and not entirely as himself — there are two pressures braided in the residue, your brother's familiar warmth and a second, older cold that walks in his steps like a hand inside a glove. You have read the file; you have the word. Healer. Yushiro is wearing Gin north toward the thinning wall, and your sight can follow them straight to it, faster than any faction's procedure, if you are willing to keep the registers open through streets that are getting less and less obliged to hold you up.

choices.x: Push the sight harder to close the distance before dawn.
choices.hint: Burn bright and you'll be at the wall by morning, ahead of every road that started with paperwork. Each push files the grammar of the world down thinner around you; by dawn you may not trust your own feet to know a platform from a corridor.

choices.x: Ration the sight — reach, fix a bearing, fold shut, walk blind, repeat.
choices.hint: Pulsing the Gift keeps the Madness from compounding, but the residue cools between pulses and you may lose the braid where it crosses water or a crowd. Lose it once and you start again from a colder trail.

choices.x: Stop and warn yourself onto paper — write down what's real before you forget it's a question.
choices.hint: Anchoring to a notebook of plain facts is the oldest trick the gifted use against the Madness. It costs you an hour and the warmth of the trail, and it admits, in your own handwriting, that you no longer fully trust your own mind.

beats.scene: A shuttered laundromat in Kita-ku where the residue pools instead of passing
prose: The trail does not end so much as gather, the way water gathers at the low point of a floor, in a closed coin laundromat with its shutter down and its machines dark and a smell of detergent gone sweet with disuse. Gin stood here a long time, more than once, and not alone; the braid of warm and cold thickens until the room in your sight is nearly solid with it, and you understand you have found one of the places where Yushiro does his reasonable work — a quiet door, off any file, where the Healer meets the people he is going to help. To read it fully is to know who has been here and what was promised them. To read it fully is also the deepest reach you have made tonight, into worked air, against a threshold someone with far more skill than you has handled, and you can feel before you start that this one will not come cheap.

You crouch and put your palm to the cold floor and open both registers wider than you have ever let them go, and the room gives itself up. Names. A widow whose husband walked back out of his coffin three days early and now answers to a different cadence. A boy who was drowning and isn't, who owes a debt he wasn't told the size of. Gin, sitting in the plastic chair by the dead machines, lucid for one window in a hundred, writing something small in a margin with a pencil and weeping without seeming to know he was. You see it all in the single overexposed instant it costs, and the cost arrives a half-second behind the seeing, the way thunder follows the light.

When it lands, the laundromat doubles. For one long terrible breath there are two of every machine, two shutters, two of you crouched on the floor, and you cannot tell which set of doors is the one your body can walk through — the Madness has stopped being a pressure and become a question you are inside of. You have the names. You have the place. You have, written behind your eyes, the whole shape of how your brother is being used. You also have, for the first time, the genuine and specific fear that you have spent something here you are not going to get back, and that the next reach might not double the room but quarter you.

choices.x: Hold the double and read which world the real door is in.
choices.hint: Reach again, into the split itself, and you can resolve which laundromat is true — but reaching while doubled is reaching from inside the Madness, and the gifted who do it sometimes resolve the wrong way and never come back to the door their body is standing at.

choices.x: Close your eyes, breathe, let the double collapse on its own.
choices.hint: Wait it out and the room will usually settle to one, costing you nothing but minutes and nerve. Usually. You will be sitting blind on the floor of a place that belongs to the thing wearing your brother while you wait to find out.

choices.x: Crawl for the shutter you remember from before you reached.
choices.hint: Trust memory over sight and move on muscle, not the Gift. It might take you to the real door; it might take you to the remembered one, which the reach has just taught you is not always the same thing.

beats.scene: Dawn, a konbini, and a man in an unremarkable coat who orders the same coffee you do
prose: You come down off the night in the white light of a convenience store because it is the only place open and the only place that feels obligated to be real, and you are three sips into a canned coffee when you notice the man by the magazines is reading you the way the woman in Sugamo read you off her cats. He is unremarkable in the studied way that is itself a uniform — good coat, no logo, the posture of someone whose job is to be forgettable — and when he turns he does not pretend he wasn't looking. You lit up the northern grid like a flare around two a.m., he says, conversationally, the way you'd remark on weather. Three of our passive arrays in Kita. We don't get readings like that off licensed practitioners. Licensed practitioners are taught not to.

He is Directorate. Not the kind with a van and a writ — the other kind, the quiet census-taker whose whole function is to find the gifted before the gifted find out what they are, and to offer them, very reasonably, a choice between a leash and a cell dressed up as a leash. He knows what you did at the laundromat the way a coastguard knows a flare went up: not the words on it, but the size of the hand that lit it. He does not, yet, know your name, or whose face you wear, or that the flare was lit looking for a man the Directorate's own file says it has stopped looking for. He is here to find out, over coffee, in the most civil way the state has, and everything you say next teaches him something.

And here is the road's cruelty laid bare: the very brightness that let you outrun every faction's procedure is the brightness that put you on the map you were trying to stay off. You spent the night becoming exactly visible to the one organisation that collects people like you. The trail is still warm in your head. The wall is close. But there is now a man in an unremarkable coat between you and it, holding a coffee, waiting, and the only tools you have to get past him are the truth, a lie, or the Gift that called him here in the first place.

choices.x: Tell him the truth — your brother, the wall, the Healer, all of it.
choices.hint: Honesty might buy a powerful ally with arrays you could never match. It also hands the Directorate a live thread straight to Gin, and the Directorate's mercy toward a recruited demon's brother is a thing you'd be betting Gin's remaining mind on.

choices.x: Lie low and small — a frightened amateur who didn't know what she did.
choices.hint: Play the unaware sensitive and he may file you as harmless and let you walk. He reads people for a living; if the lie cracks, you've taught the census-taker that you lie under pressure, which is the one fact he most wanted.

choices.x: Reach, find his own thresholds, and let him feel you read him back.
choices.hint: Show him you can do to him what he does to others and he may decide you're not worth the paperwork. It is also the loudest possible flare, fired point-blank at the array that walks on two legs, and it tells the Axis there is a new bright thing in the city worth collecting.

beats.scene: A Directorate intake room that is trying very hard to look like an ordinary office
prose: However the coffee ends, the road bends you through a room like this one, because brightness has a gravity and the Directorate is where it pools. The intake room has soft chairs and a plant and a window with a pleasant view, and all of it is a sentence constructed to make you forget you cannot leave until someone decides you can. A woman with a lanyard and a kind, tired face slides a form across the table — a licensing application, she calls it, though the word license is doing the work of three uglier words — and explains, reasonably, that an unregistered practitioner who flares the northern arrays is a danger primarily to herself. The veil, she says, does not care whose sanity it spends. She has watched gifted people burn out into the Madness and she would rather you didn't. You believe her, which is the trap; the leash is being offered by someone who genuinely does not want you to die on the end of your own Gift.

What the form does not say, in any of its boxes, is that a licensed practitioner reaches only when and where the Directorate permits, logs every reach, and is therefore reachable in turn — a flare the state can see, aim, and if necessary extinguish. Sign, and you get training that might keep the Madness at bay long enough to reach the wall sane. Sign, and your every future reach toward your brother happens inside a system that has already closed his case and would dearly like to know why you keep opening it. The kind tired woman is not lying to you. She has simply been issued a leash and told it is a hand, and over enough years she has come to hold it the same way.

You can feel the road forking under the table. There is a version of you that signs, and learns, and reaches the wall as a sanctioned, surveilled, surviving practitioner who has traded freedom for the years the Gift would otherwise burn. There is a version that does not sign, and walks out, and reaches the wall as a flare nobody can aim — brighter, freer, and on a fuse you can already feel shortening. Both versions are looking for the same brother. Only one of them will still be entirely themselves when they find him, and you cannot yet tell which.

choices.x: Sign. Take the training, the leash, and the years it buys.
choices.hint: A license might keep you sane enough to reach the wall and recognise Gin when you get there. Every reach you make after this is logged, aimable, and made in a system that wants Gin's case to stay closed — including the reach where you finally find him.

choices.x: Refuse, politely, and walk out unlicensed and unaimed.
choices.hint: Keep your freedom and your fuse. You leave as a flare the Directorate can see but not steer, which makes you useful to exactly one party in this city: whoever is collecting bright unaligned things, and they are not the Directorate.

choices.x: Refuse, and take the training notes off the table on your way out.
choices.hint: Steal the anti-Madness craft without the leash that's supposed to come with it. You'll learn to reach safer on your own terms — and you'll have made, in writing, an enemy of the one faction whose arrays could have found Gin if you'd let them.

beats.scene: The painter's loft, because the only person who survived the Gift untrained is the one the Tower threw back
prose: There is a name the Directorate woman did not write on any form, because the Directorate does not like to admit it exists: a practitioner who carries a Gift that came in sideways, never licensed, never caged, and somehow not yet burned out — Itsuki, who paints, whose sight arrives through pigment and a cut palm and who left a house that measures its children against a stone older than the city. You find the loft because the Grid's margins point at it and because, when you reach for the brightest unaligned thing in the northern city that isn't you, it is here. Itsuki opens the door already knowing what you are; you are both lit, and two lit people in a doorway is a kind of recognition that does not need names.

Itsuki has done the thing you are deciding whether to do — lived gifted and unleashed — and the loft is the evidence of the cost and the survival both. There are canvases turned to the wall that you are asked not to look at, and you understand without being told that they are reaches Itsuki made and could not unmake, the Madness given a frame so it would stay in the frame. You're reaching too hard, too fast, Itsuki says, not unkindly, looking at you the way the woman in Sugamo looked at her cats. I can see the thin spots. You've been doubling rooms. Another week like the night you just had and you won't come back from a double — you'll just pick the wrong door, calmly, and be gone, and your body will walk on. It is the first time anyone has named your specific death to your face, and it is offered as help.

What Itsuki offers is craft — how to reach without the veil thinning so fast, how to bleed a little of the Madness onto a canvas instead of into your skull, how to find your brother bright and stay yourself doing it. What Itsuki asks in return is honesty, the thing the gifted trade in: that you say plainly what you are reaching for and what it will cost the people you reach through. The road has given you a teacher at the exact moment the Madness made one a matter of survival — and a teacher is a tie, and a tie is a place where another person can be hurt to move you, which is precisely how the Healer prefers to work.

choices.x: Accept the teaching, and tell Itsuki everything — Gin, the wall, the cost.
choices.hint: Itsuki's craft might be the only thing that gets you to the wall sane. Telling the truth makes Itsuki a thread the Healer can pull, and you have just watched, all night, how gently and reasonably this enemy pulls threads.

choices.x: Take the craft, give Itsuki only half the truth.
choices.hint: Learn to survive the Gift without handing over a hostage. Itsuki trades in honesty; a half-truth between two lit people is a thin spot the other can see, and you'll be learning sanity from someone who has just learned you'll lie to them.

choices.x: Refuse the teaching — you don't have a week to spend learning to go slow.
choices.hint: Stay fast, stay bright, reach the wall before the Madness catches you. You will arrive ahead of everyone and on the exact fuse Itsuki just told you, to your face, ends with you picking the wrong door.

beats.scene: The threshold of the thinning wall, where bright things are noticed from the other side
prose: You reach the wall the way only this road could bring you — not led there by a faction, not handed an address, but having tracked your own brother across a thinning city with your own sight until the trail and the wall and the cost all arrive at the same point. And the wall, when you stand at it with both registers open, is the most beautiful and the most wrong thing you have ever seen: a place where the membrane between this side and the other has been worked thin, deliberately, lovingly, by someone who calls the thinning a healing. You can read the whole plan off it now, whole, the way the road promised — the seats, the vacant Thirteenth, the membrane drawn down to let something cross and take a chair that has stood empty too long. You did not have to learn the seam by ear, one stolen lucid sentence at a time. You burned your way to seeing it entire.

But the road has its final, quiet cruelty, and it is this: the things on the other side of a thinning wall can see bright things on this side, and you have spent the entire road making yourself the brightest thing in northern Tokyo. The Axis does not have a stair because the Axis is not a place you go; it is the gravity that bright gifted things fall into, the machinery around the empty seat that collects whatever flares near it, and you have been flaring straight at it since the kitchen. Standing at the wall you feel it notice you — not Yushiro, not yet, but the seat itself, the vacancy, turning its empty attention toward the new light like a cold eye opening. You came to read your brother's situation. You have made yourself legible to the very thing his captor is feeding.

And then, through the worked-thin air, a familiar warmth finds you, and for one window the size of a held breath it is just Gin — lucid, horrified, reaching back across the seam not to pull you through but to push you away, his cold passenger asleep or distracted or simply outvoted for one human second. You shouldn't be this bright, he tells you, in the only language the wall leaves him, and you understand it is both the most loving and the most frightened thing your brother has ever said to you. You have found him. He has found you. And the finding, done this brightly, this close to the seat, has put you both exactly where the Healer would most like you to be: in the same place, lit, legible, and reachable through each other.

choices.x: Reach back to Gin through the window — answer him while it's open.
choices.hint: One true exchange with your brother, mind to mind, might give you the seam from the inside and a thread of him to hold. It is also the brightest possible flare fired directly at the wall, in full view of the seat that just opened its eye, using the one channel the Healer most wants mapped.

choices.x: Damp yourself down — fold the registers, go dark at the wall.
choices.hint: Go quiet now and you may slip the Axis's attention before it fixes on you. Folding shut here means losing the window with Gin, perhaps the last lucid one, and walking blind back into a city you can no longer fully read.

choices.x: Step toward the wall while it's thin and you're bright enough to cross.
choices.hint: Brightness this close to a worked membrane might be enough to step through and reach Gin in the flesh. Crossing a thinned wall toward the empty seat is exactly the motion the Healer engineered the whole membrane to invite — you would be walking, lit, into the trap as its final piece.

look.title: The Long Walk
acts: Open: the city decides for you
Deepen: what the short ways step over
Converge: arriving without a faction at your back

beats.scene: The kitchen, 3:47 on the stove clock, and the decision to take nothing but your feet
prose: There are five ways out of this room and four of them ask you to spend something you can't get back — a name handed to a badge, a favour owed to the Grid, the registers behind your eyes pried open until the world goes thin around you. You stand in the cooling kitchen with the rice still warm in the cooker and you understand, with the flat certainty that arrives only at four in the morning, that you are going to refuse all four. You are going to do the slow, stupid, human thing. You are going to walk out the door with nothing in your hands and look for your brother the way a person looks for a person.

It is not nobility. You want to be honest with yourself about that much while you still can be. It is fear — fear of the badge, which keeps what it touches; fear of the Gift, which keeps the one who uses it; fear most of all of becoming, in the search for Gin, the kind of thing Gin would no longer recognise as his sibling. The other roads are faster and you can feel the speed of them pulling at you like a draft under the door. But fast is how he was taken. Fast is the seam in the air at chest height where something stepped through that should not be able to step through anything. You decide, in the dark, that whatever has him moves at the speed of taking, and you will move at the speed of finding, and you will trust that the second speed reaches further in the end.

So you do the small things a person does. You write a note for the family that says less than you know. You put on shoes that can take a night of pavement. You leave the rice. And at the genkan you stop with your hand on the door and feel the absence of everything the other roads would have armed you with — no procedure, no protection, no sight — and you step out into the Obon dark anyway, into a Tokyo lit for the returning dead, with nothing to find your living brother but attention and time.

choices.x: Leave now, in the dark, before you can talk yourself onto a faster road.
choices.hint: Move while the trail is warm and you'll be on the streets ahead of the dawn crowds. You also leave with no money plan, no contact, and no idea how many nights this costs — the long walk has no timetable, and Gin's lucid windows do.

choices.x: Wait for first light and gather what a traveller needs — cash, a map, his photo.
choices.hint: An hour of preparation makes the walk survivable for days instead of one. Every hour you spend packing is an hour the thing wearing your brother spends walking him north.

choices.x: Knock on one door first — wake someone who loved Gin and ask before the city wakes.
choices.hint: A second pair of eyes and a second memory could halve the search. It also means letting another person into a danger you chose to face alone precisely so no one else would have to.

beats.scene: The last trains gone, the night city of Obon, choosing a direction by ordinary signs
prose: Without the sight you have no line of cooling footprints to follow, and at first the loss of it is vertiginous — you keep reaching for a sense you've decided not to use, the way a tongue keeps finding the gap of a pulled tooth. But the city is not silent to ordinary eyes; it is only quieter, and slower, and you have to learn its plainer language fast. A man your brother's height was seen, or wasn't. A timetable on the kitchen shelf was folded back to the Kita line. A cab driver at the Sugamo rank remembers a fare who didn't speak and didn't seem to know where he was going, only north, always a little further north, as if north were a person calling him.

This is the road's whole discipline and you feel it close around you like a habit: you cannot leap, so you must accumulate. Each scrap is nearly nothing — a direction, a time, the colour of a coat — and only by laying them end to end across a night of walking do they become a thread you can pull. You walk Hakusan-dori with the lanterns swinging overhead, the families home for Obon eating late, the smell of grilling and incense and rain that hasn't fallen yet, and you do the arithmetic of the ordinary: who would have been awake, who would have seen, who would tell a stranger the truth at this hour. The dead are supposedly walking these same streets tonight, come home for the festival. You find you are not afraid of them. You are afraid of being too slow for the one who isn't dead yet.

By the third hour your feet have begun to hurt in the specific, instructive way that tells you this is real now, this is your body spent on this and not retrievable, and somewhere under the tiredness you notice the first quiet gift of the slow road: you are still entirely yourself. No register has opened. Nothing on the other side of anything has turned to look at you.
