And then, before you can answer, her eyes go to the one cage she has not offered you, low in the corner, where something old and brown lies with its nose to the bars and has not once looked away from the door you came in through.

choices.x: "Show me the steady ones. I work alone — I could use an instrument I can trust."
choices.hint: Komori will sell you a good medium, and it will help, and you will spend the rest of the case feeling the small kept-open wound of it against your own register every time you reach. An instrument that works because someone hollowed it gentle — and you would be the someone now.

choices.x: "The one in the corner. The one you didn't offer me. What is it waiting for?"
choices.hint: She didn't offer it because it can't be sold, and asking means asking about a grief she keeps in a cage by the door — and once you know what it's waiting for, the not-helping becomes a thing you chose.

choices.x: Read the cages first — let your sight tell you what each animal is carrying before money is mentioned.
choices.hint: Reading hollowed things this close, this many at once, opens both registers wider than a backstreet can hold, and the festival has already thinned the air outside. You'll know exactly what you're buying — and everything in the room will know it's being read.

beats.scene: The corner cage, the brown dog lifting its head only enough to be sure you are not the one it is waiting for
prose: Her name is Tsuyu, Komori says, which means the dew, the kind that is gone by the time anyone wakes to see it, and she is older than she looks and was never meant to be a stock animal at all. She belonged to a man named Asano, an unregistered sensitive who worked the Kita line and trained her himself, slow and kind, to hold one thread at a time and give it back unbroken — a courier's dog for messages the dead leave half-spoken. Eleven nights ago Asano walked north and did not come back, and a neighbour brought Tsuyu here because the shop is where the district's hollow animals come to die quietly, and she has not eaten properly since and will not be re-homed, because she is not finished with the job he gave her: she is still holding his thread, the last one, waiting to give it to the only hands she was trained to give it to.

You crouch to the bars and she does not warm to you, which is correct — she is a professional, and you are not her handler — but she lets you close enough to feel it, and it is unmistakable. There is a passenger in her still, faint, frayed at the edge the way a thread frays when the other end has been pulled too far away too fast, and it is unmistakably a man, and unmistakably going. Komori has tried to ease it out of her the way she eases the others, so the cage might be useful again, and Tsuyu has refused every time, clamping down on the fading thing inside her like a dog refusing to drop a stick, because dropping it is the one thing Asano never taught her and the one thing she will not do without him. She'll die holding it, Komori says, without cruelty, only accounting. That's not loyalty. That's a job that never got a stop word.

And here is the shape of it, cold and exact: the thread Tsuyu is holding is Asano, or the last of him she could keep, and Asano went north in Obon, alone and unregistered and uncounted — the exact profile of the tidying you have been reading the edges of for days, the half-touched and the unguarded swept gentle up the Kita line toward the thinning wall by a familiar warmth that makes the leaving feel like being led home. You did not come here for the spine of your own case. You came for an instrument. But the corner cage has handed you a witness instead — a witness with no words, no file, no admissibility, who watched a man be invited north and has been holding the proof against her ribs ever since, waiting for hands steady enough to take it without breaking it.

choices.x: Open your registers and take the thread from her — read Asano's last walk the way she's been holding it.
choices.hint: She was trained to give it to her handler, not to you; taking it means convincing a grieving animal you are close enough to count, and reading a man's frayed last hour will pull it through you the way the river pulled Kase. You'd get the clearest map yet of how the tidying is done — paid for in a register held open over a dying dog.

choices.x: Don't take it. Sit with her until she chooses — let the dog decide whether you're the steady hands.
choices.hint: Patience is the honest way and the slow way, and the thread is fraying while you wait; she may finish dying before she trusts you, and then the proof and the dog go out together. The kindest road may cost you the witness entirely.

choices.x: Ask Komori to ease it out the way she eases the others, cleanly, and let Tsuyu rest.
choices.hint: It would end her suffering and free the cage — and it would scrape the last of Asano off the one surface he survived on, close the only window onto his walk north, and teach you that mercy and erasure can be the same gesture done at the right angle.

beats.scene: The thread, given or taken or refused — and the cold clear sense of where it leads
prose: If you reached for it, Tsuyu does not fight you the way she fought Komori; she has been waiting eleven nights for hands that feel like the work, and yours, opened wide and unafraid of the hollow in her, feel close enough. The thread comes across into you whole and frayed, and for the length of one held breath you are Asano on his last walk — not his memories, his going, the particular footstep-by-footstep ease of a man who never noticed he'd decided to leave, drawn north past the embankment by a warmth he took for a friend's, the lanterns kind, the streets obliging, the whole night arranged so that walking away from his own life felt exactly like walking home. You feel where the obliging stopped. You feel the half-second of late air. You feel him think, once, of the dog — and then the thread ends, not cut, just arrived somewhere you cannot follow on foot, and you come back to the cage with the map of the tidying drawn in a dead man's gait and a dog going slack with eleven nights of finished waiting under your hands.

If you sat and waited, the choice was hers, and dogs are not generous with strangers — but Tsuyu is a professional, and somewhere in the long quiet she weighs you against the only handler she ever had and decides you are not him but you are the work, and she gives it the only way she has left, by laying her head against your sternum and simply letting go, the thread passing the way warmth passes between two bodies in the cold. You get less of it this way, no walk, no map, only the shape of the leaving — gentle, invited, northward — but you get it clean, unforced, a witness's testimony freely given, and you get the weight of having been chosen by something that had every reason to die distrustful and didn't.

If you asked Komori to ease her, the old woman does it with hands that have done it a hundred times, and it is quiet and it is kind and it is the wrong kind, and you watch the last of Asano go out of the dog like breath off a mirror — not delivered, not witnessed, just tidied, the same verb the thing up north uses, done now by your own request in a borrowed back room. The cage will be useful again. Tsuyu sleeps and does not wake afraid. And you understand, standing in the borrowed dark, that you have just learned the precise feeling of choosing the clean erasure over the costly witness, and that the feeling is exactly as comfortable as Komori warned you the easy mediums would be, and that you will recognise it now every time the fast road offers it to you again.

choices.x: Follow the map north as far as a living person can — verify where Asano's walk ended.
choices.hint: The thread points at the thinning wall, the same edge your brother is being walked toward; following it means lighting yourself up on the Kita line again, brighter and closer, exactly where the Healer would most like a searching sensitive to be.

choices.x: Take what you have to Tanizaki and the others — make Asano count as evidence, uncounted as he was.
choices.hint: A dog's thread is admissible nowhere, but it corroborates the tidying, and pooling it with Kase and the broker's census builds the one case no single faction can dismiss — at the cost of telling people you trust exactly how bright you let yourself burn to get it.

choices.x: Keep it to yourself for now — carry the dog, or her absence, and say nothing.
choices.hint: Holding the only witness alone keeps it from being spent by a faction's agenda, and it also means the weight of Asano's leaving sits entirely in you, one more uncounted soul you took responsibility for that no one asked you to save.

beats.scene: Suzuran-dō, the leaving — Komori counting what the night actually cost
prose: Komori does not thank you, because thanks are a thing you spend and she has spent enough on you already, but she walks you to the mouth of the shop, which she does not do for everyone, and she looks at you in the borrowed lantern-light the way she looked at the cages, reading the small new emptiness in you that was not there an hour ago. You took it like a handler, she says, if you reached; or she gave it to you, which she's never done, if you waited; or you chose the kind way, and you'll choose it again, if you asked her to ease it — and in each version it is not quite praise and not quite warning, only the flat accounting of a woman who has watched a great many people learn what they are by what they were willing to do to a dog in a corner cage.

She will not sell you one of the steady ones now. You have shown her the only thing she sells to, she says, which is the difference between someone who feels the kept-open wound and someone who would keep it open for their own convenience, and she has decided which you are, and the deciding is the whole transaction — the mediums were never really for sale, the way the best things in Kita are never really for sale, only offered to see what you'll do. If you ever come back, she tells you, come back for an animal you mean to be the handler of, not an instrument you mean to use, and shut the door on your way out, because the festival is leaning wrong tonight and she would rather the cold stayed in the street where it belongs.

Out in the alley the lanterns are doing their patient work of making a thinned city look like somewhere it is safe to gather, and you carry the night's weight north or homeward or nowhere, depending. Whatever you did with Tsuyu, you came for an instrument and left with a witness, or with the knowledge of having silenced one, and both registers have gone quiet in the particular way they go quiet after they have been made to understand something the easy road would have let you skip. Eleven nights ago a man walked north and felt like he was going home. A dog held the proof against her ribs until hands steady enough came. The only question Obon leaves you, turning out of the backstreet, is whether you will let what she held make the case — or let it be one more gentle, uncounted erasure in a season that is full of them.

choices.x: North — let the thread point you back toward the spine, toward Gin.
choices.hint: It feeds the main search, and it feeds it with you brighter and surer of the route than ever, which is precisely the condition under which the Healer's whole plan works best.

choices.x: Home, for now — set the weight down before it sets the terms.
choices.hint: Resting is the sane choice and the slow one; the thinning does not rest, and the part of you that took a dying dog's last thread will be awake at two in the morning whether you are or not.

choices.x: Back to the others — make Asano count, and let them see what counting him cost you.
choices.hint: The case grows; so does the number of people who now know exactly how far you'll open yourself to find your brother, and knowing it, will worry about it, and may try to stop you.

sideMissions.title: The Shrine That Stopped Answering
sideMissions.hook: The wards have held for a century; this week the basin's water stopped reflecting the lanterns.

beats.scene: The Hozumi shrine in upper Kita, third morning of Obon — a fox-shrine the size of a shed, wedged between a parking tower and a shuttered noodle counter, and Miyamoto Kazuo waiting at the gate before you have finished climbing the steps
prose: The old man is sweeping when you arrive, which is the first wrong thing, because the stones are already clean and he is sweeping them anyway — the slow, going-nowhere stroke of a man keeping his hands busy so they will not shake. Miyamoto Kazuo has tended this shrine for fifty-one years and his father tended it before him and the wards that ring the precinct were renewed by a hand in his line every Obon for a hundred summers, and he tells you all of this without your asking, the way a man recites the deed to a house he is afraid is no longer his. The shrine is nothing — two fox statues with the lichen grown into their grins, a vermilion gate gone the colour of dried blood, a basin of standing water under a little roof where you are meant to rinse your hands before you bother the god. It is the kind of place the city forgets so thoroughly that forgetting it becomes its own kind of protection.

He will not let you near the basin until he has said the thing he called you to say, and he says it badly, in pieces, looking at the broom and not at you. For a hundred years the water in that basin has held the lanterns — every Obon the neighbourhood strings paper lights along the lane, and every Obon the basin catches them and holds them doubled and trembling on its skin, and that doubling, Miyamoto says, is how you know the boundary is keeping. A shrine that reflects is a shrine that is still listening. This week the lanterns are lit and the lane is strung and the water lies in the basin flat and black and holds nothing at all — no lights, no roof-beam, not even your face when you lean, he says, when you lean over it your own face is not there.

Both registers come up at that, slow and certain, the low one and the searching one both, and they do not disagree. You have spent enough of this week learning the particular wrongness of a thing that has stopped answering — Gin's flat, the address in no file, the cases closed too clean — to recognise the shape of it in an old man's basin. Miyamoto sets the broom against the gate at last and folds his hands and tells you he is too old to read what has gone wrong and too frightened to leave it unread, that he sent word to the Tower and the Tower sent a form, that he sent word to the temple and the temple sent prayers, and that he is asking you because you are the only one who came up the steps instead of mailing something down them. Behind him the basin sits under its little roof, holding the morning the way a closed eye holds a room.

choices.x: "Tell me what the wards were keeping out — a hundred years of renewing them, your line knows the name of the thing."
choices.hint: Miyamoto will tell you what his father told him, which is old and half-liturgy and possibly true — and knowing the name of what the boundary held back means you will be looking for it now, in the water and everywhere else, the way you cannot unsee a face once it has been pointed out. Some wards are kept strong precisely by the keeper never quite knowing.

choices.x: "Who renewed the wards this Obon? You said your line does it — did you do it yourself this year?"
choices.hint: The answer is the whole mission and the old man knows it, which is why his hands are shaking; press him and he will have to say aloud whatever help he accepted this year, from whatever reasonable stranger offered it. A favour done to a hundred-year ward is a favour you cannot easily take back.

choices.x: Say nothing yet; go to the basin and read the water before he frames it for you.
choices.hint: Reading the basin cold means seeing only what the boundary itself shows, uncoloured by an old man's fear or his father's stories — the truest read you can get. It also means putting your own face over water that has stopped giving faces back, with no idea yet what is on the other side of the skin, waiting to be looked at in return.

beats.scene: The basin under its little roof, the lane's paper lanterns burning unreflected three steps away, the water holding nothing
prose: Up close the water is worse than Miyamoto described, because he described an absence and an absence is at least a clean thing, and this is not clean. The basin is full to the lip and dead still, no wind reaching it under the roof, and when you lean the lanterns behind you do not appear and neither do you, but the surface is not blank — it is busy, in the way a held breath is busy, a faint slow churn under the flatness like something turning over far down in water that is only a hand deep. You put two fingers to the stone rim, not the water, and let the read come, and the read comes wrong. A shrine basin should taste of a hundred Obons of cupped hands and rinsed mouths and small honest fears asked into the dark; this one tastes of all that and then, underneath, of a single clean cut — a place where something woven was unwoven, neatly, by someone who knew exactly which thread to lift.

You crouch and look longer than is wise, and the longer you look the more certain both registers become that the water is not failing to reflect you — it is choosing not to, the way a person who has been told something about you declines to meet your eye. Somewhere in the basin's hundred years a boundary was strung between the lane and whatever the lane was built to forget, and the boundary was kept taut by reflection, by the simple daily proof that the world on this side was solid enough to throw an image back. Pull the proof and the boundary goes slack. The lanterns burn three steps behind you, gold and doubled along the lane, and stop dead at the rim of this stone as though the basin has been excused from the evening, lifted quietly out of the week, set apart so that something can use it without the neighbourhood noticing the seam.

When you take your fingers off the rim the churn under the surface settles, slowly, the way water settles after a fish has turned — and for one held instant before it goes flat again the black skin shows you a face after all, not yours, a calm and pleasant and entirely reasonable face that you have been learning the shape of all week without yet being allowed to name it. Then the water lies still and gives nothing, and behind you Miyamoto asks, in the small voice of a man who already knows, whether you saw anything. The honest answer is that you saw the Healer's bedside manner wearing a hundred-year-old shrine like a clean white coat. The lane keeps burning. The basin keeps its peace, which is the wrong kind of peace, the kind that has been arranged.

choices.x: Read deeper — push past the flatness and follow the single clean cut to the hand that made it.
choices.hint: Following the cut means reading toward the one who unwove the ward, and you already half-know whose calm face the water just showed you — to read further is to let it read back along the same thread, to announce to the thing on the other side that someone on this side has finally looked. Your sight thins what is already thinning.

choices.x: Pull back and tell Miyamoto the truth: the ward wasn't worn down, it was opened, this year, by a hand that knew the work.
choices.hint: The old man deserves the truth and will break a little under it, because it means the help he accepted was the wound, and he will want to know who — and naming Yushiro to a frightened keeper sends the name out into the neighbourhood ahead of you, where it cannot be called back. Some truths are doors you cannot reach back through.

choices.x: Empty the basin — tip the dead water out onto the stones and refill it from the lane's tap, and see whether fresh water reflects.
choices.hint: Emptying the basin is the obvious test and possibly a mercy, restoring the daily proof that keeps the boundary taut — or it is exactly the disturbance the cut was made to invite, the keeper's own hand breaking the last still surface and letting the slack boundary swing. The thing about a trap built from a kindness is that undoing the kindness springs it.

beats.scene: Inside the shrine office, a one-mat room behind the gate, Miyamoto's ledger of renewals open on the low table under a bare bulb
prose: The ledger goes back further than the bulb, further than the table, a stack of bound books in a cloth-wrapped pile each one a generation's worth of Obons recorded in the cramped hand of whoever held the broom that century. Miyamoto turns to this year's page with the reluctance of a man opening a wound to show the doctor where it hurts, and the entry is there in an unfamiliar hand — not his, not his line's, a clean modern script that has written, in the place where the keeper records who renewed the wards, the single word that means *a friend assisted*. He came in the spring, Miyamoto says, looking at the foreign handwriting in his family's book. A soft-spoken man, a healer he said, who had heard the old keeper's hands were failing and offered, for nothing, for the simple rightness of it, to help renew the work his father could no longer manage. He was so kind, Miyamoto says, and his voice does the thing voices do when kindness turns out to have been the knife. He was so very kind, and he asked only that I let him tie the last knot himself, because the last knot, he said, is the one that matters.

You read the foreign entry and both registers go cold and quiet, because you have seen this hand before — or its work, the same neat economy, the same gift offered into exactly the gap a person is most ashamed of — in Gin's ledger of favours, in every place this week where Yushiro the Healer has reached in through someone's worst small fear and adjusted one thread while they wept with gratitude. The wards were not breached. They were *re-tied*, expertly, by a guest invited in through the front gate by the keeper's own grief at his failing hands, and the last knot — the one that holds the reflection, the one that keeps the boundary listening — was tied to give way on a schedule. This week. Obon, when the membrane over all of Kita is thinnest and every shrine in the district is straining to hold its own small portion of the wall. Pull one keeper's stone loose now and you do not get a flood. You get a draught, a single clean current through one forgotten shed of a shrine, feeding the larger thinning Yushiro has been working toward all along.

Miyamoto wants to know what you will do, and under that, what he did, whether his failing hands made this or whether it would have come anyway — and there is no answer you can give that returns the spring to him, the morning he was so grateful to be helped. You can re-tie the last knot yourself and close the draught, which costs the neighbourhood nothing and costs you the one open window you currently have onto what Yushiro is building, a window the Healer does not yet know you have found. Or you can leave it open and watched, let the shrine keep failing on its arranged schedule, and learn from this small clean current exactly where the larger thinning runs and what it is for — at the price of an old man's basin, and the boundary his line kept for a hundred years, and whatever uses a draught while you stand at it taking notes.

choices.x: Re-tie the last knot now — close the draught, restore the reflection, and give the old man his shrine back.
choices.hint: Closing it is the clean kindness and the right one by Miyamoto, and it shuts a wound in the membrane before whatever wants through gets through. It also blinds you: the one place you can currently watch Yushiro's plan operate goes dark, and the Healer learns nothing was missed — which means the next stone he loosens, you will not be standing over when it gives.

choices.x: Leave it open but ward the keeper — seal Miyamoto out of the precinct, let the draught run watched, and trace where the current pulls.
choices.hint: A watched draught is intelligence you cannot get any other way, a live thread back into the thinning while the Healer still believes it unobserved — but you are choosing to let a hundred-year boundary stay open, with an old man exiled from the shrine his family kept, and you do not fully know what a single clean current into Kita this week is meant to feed, or whether watching it counts, to the thing on the other side, as an introduction.

choices.x: Re-tie the knot but tie it wrong on purpose — close it to all eyes but yours, a knot only you can read, so the draught looks shut and isn't.
choices.hint: The clever middle path: the shrine reflects again, Miyamoto sleeps, the Healer sees his work apparently undone by ordinary decay — and you keep a private window the size of a keyhole. But a knot tied by your two suppressed registers is a knot with your name woven into it, hung in the one place Yushiro is certain to come back and check, and a healer reads handwriting better than anyone alive.

beats.scene: The lane at dusk, lanterns lit, the basin's verdict settling — and Miyamoto at the gate waiting to learn what his hundred years come to
prose: Whatever you chose, the evening insists on happening: the neighbourhood comes out as it always does on the third night, old women in cotton yukata and children with their fox-masks pushed up on their foreheads, and they file past the little shrine and clap their twice and bow and do not feel the seam you have spent the day standing inside. That is the mercy and the horror of a forgotten shrine — its failing is invisible to exactly the people it fails, and the boundary your day's work either closed or kept open holds back a thing none of them will ever be asked to believe in. The lanterns are doubled along the lane in their gold strings, and now, depending on the knot, the basin either catches them and holds them trembling on its skin the way it has for a hundred summers, or it lies flat and black and apart, excused from the evening, holding its arranged peace.

Miyamoto finds you at the gate and reads your face before you speak, the way old keepers read water, and what passes between you is not gratitude exactly — you have not given him back the spring, the morning he was glad to be helped, and both of you know the kind stranger will come again to some other failing pair of hands with the same soft offer and the same patient knot. But he takes your hand in both of his, dry and light as paper, and tells you that his father used to say the shrine does not protect the neighbourhood from the thing on the other side; it protects the thing on the other side from the neighbourhood's forgetting, keeps it small and named and bounded, because a forgotten thing grows and a watched thing waits. You have either restored the watching or volunteered to be the watcher. The Healer, somewhere across the thinning city, has either lost one quiet draught or gained, without yet knowing it, one observer at the seam — and either way he is one stone further along a wall he means to bring down by Obon's end.

You go down the steps as the drums start somewhere toward the river, the slow Obon rhythm that calls the dead home for their three nights and sends them off again, and the sound finds the loose thing in you that has been pulled tight all day. A shrine that stopped answering has been made to answer again, or made to answer only to you, or let alone to teach you the shape of the larger silence — and any of those is a hand laid on the same wall your brother's keeper Gin once helped tend, and that Gin, worn thin and wearing a healer's calm, is now helping to thin. The lane burns gold behind you. Down at the embankment, the first paper boats go onto the black water, holding their small lights out for the dead, and the dead this week are very close, and getting closer, by exactly as many stones as the Healer can talk a grieving keeper into loosening.

choices.x: Take the foreign ledger-page to Tanizaki — the Healer's handwriting is evidence, and the old fixer can read a hand across a city.
choices.hint: Carrying the page to Tanizaki turns one shrine's wound into a thread you can pull on the spine itself — proof, in Yushiro's own script, of how the thinning is being worked. But it also means the shrine's quiet trouble becomes part of the loud thing you are chasing, and a healer who learns his handwriting is being collected starts writing in other hands.

choices.x: Tell no one; fold the shrine into the small private map of loosened stones you are building, and keep watching for the next one.
choices.hint: Keeping it private keeps it yours and keeps the Healer unalarmed, and lets you build, stone by stone, the actual shape of the wall he means to drop — the most valuable thing you could carry into the Vacant Seat. But a map you tell no one about is a weight you carry alone toward a two-demon trap, and the last keeper who tried to hold the whole wall in his own two failing hands is sweeping clean stones at a basin that only just started reflecting again.

sideMissions.title: Kaneda's Last Bottle
sideMissions.hook: A bar owner's final bottle of his late wife's plum wine keeps refilling itself a finger overnight. Grief, an anchored spirit, and a man who would rather be haunted than healed.

beats.scene: The honest table, an hour before open
prose: Kaneda's place is six stools and a counter the colour of long use, down a Jūjō side-street where the vending machines hum the only light. He lets you in before open because Gin's name still works like a key in this part of the city, and he sets a cup of barley tea in front of you without asking, the way a man does when he has decided to talk and needs his hands busy first. You read the room before he says anything — you cannot help it, the way you cannot help hearing your own pulse — and the room reads back grief, but the clean kind, the kind that has been folded and put away and taken out only on the right nights. It is not the room that is wrong. It is the bottle behind him, on the high shelf, where the light does not reach and something nonetheless keeps a small, patient account.

He pours you nothing, because the bottle is not for pouring. Sachiko made it, he says, and the name comes out worn smooth. Plum wine, the last batch she put up the summer before the stroke, eleven jars that became ten that became one, drunk down over six years of anniversaries to the width of two fingers in the bottom of the glass. Two fingers, he says again, and looks at it, and you watch him not reach for it. I measured it. I marked the glass. I am not a superstitious man, Uedera-kun. I marked the glass with a grease pencil and I went to bed and in the morning there were three fingers, and I have not slept right since.

choices.x: Read the bottle directly — throw your sight at it.
choices.hint: The fast knowledge. Objects hold contact-history; this one held her hands for a whole summer. Reading it will tell you what is anchored here — and announce, to anything listening on the other side, that a strong unmanaged aperture just opened in the room.

choices.x: Ask him what he wants to happen.
choices.hint: The slow, decent question, and the one that complicates everything. A man who marks a glass and keeps it is not always a man who wants the measuring to stop.

beats.scene: What the glass remembers
prose: Whichever way you come to it, the bottle resolves under your attention like a held breath. There is no demon here and no suffering-being weight, none of the deposited dread that makes a Nerima stairwell unbearable; there is a person, thin and intact and gentle, anchored not to the bar and not to Kaneda but to the wine itself — to the one object in the world that still holds the work of her hands. Register I, grief, the most common and the most misread: a spirit that does not haunt so much as wait, deepening the sorrow already in a place without ever intending harm, the way a low note under a song makes the whole song heavier. She is topping the bottle up. You feel it the moment you understand it, and the understanding is unbearably tender: she is not draining anything, not feeding, not asking. She is filling the glass back toward full because for forty years that is what she did when his cup got low, and death changed the medium and not the habit.

It is the kindest haunting you have ever read and it is killing him by inches, which is the part the official framework gets wrong about grief-register spirits and the part you understand in your own chest before you can put it in words. Every morning he wakes to proof that she is still tending him. Every morning he cannot drink the proof, because to drink it would be to lower the level she keeps raising, and so the one bottle that should have run out and let him grieve cleanly will now, gently, lovingly, never empty, and he will stand behind that counter being cared for by his dead wife until it hollows him out completely. The cruelty is that nothing here is cruel.

choices.x: Tell Kaneda exactly what you read — all of it.
choices.hint: The truth he is owed and may not survive whole. To name her is to make her real to him in a way the grease-pencil mark let him keep at arm's length.

choices.x: Tell him only that it is harmless, and buy yourself time to think.
choices.hint: A mercy and a small lie of omission. You would be deciding, for a grown man, how much of his own haunting he gets to know — the exact thing the bureaus do, that you have always hated them for.

choices.x: Say nothing yet; find out if she can be spoken to.
choices.hint: Spirits with intact selves can sometimes be reached. But reaching her means opening further, here, in a thin district during Obon — and a grief-anchor that learns it has been noticed does not always stay gentle.

beats.scene: The thing he will not say he wants
prose: You get it out of him eventually, the way you get the true thing out of anyone, by being quiet longer than is comfortable. He does not want her gone. Of course he does not. He has spent six years drinking a bottle down so that the drinking would be a thing he did with her, one anniversary at a time, and the prospect of an empty bottle was never relief — it was the second funeral, the real one, the one where the last work of her hands finally passed through him and out of the world. The refilling terrifies him and he would not trade it for anything. If you make it stop, he says, not as a threat, just as a man laying his cards face up on his own honest table, then I have to bury her again, and I am not — I don't think I am — and he does not finish it, and the unfinished part is the whole job.

This is the place where your two registers pull opposite ways and you feel both of them, the searching one and the suppressed one, the part of you that wants to fix and the part of you that knows fixing is sometimes just tidying away another person's love because it makes you uncomfortable to watch it cost them. Gin would have known what to do here. Gin always knew the difference between a haunting that harms and a haunting that merely hurts, and you are starting to understand that the difference is not in the spirit at all. It is in whether the living one has finished needing it. Kaneda has not finished. The bottle is the only place his hands and hers still meet.

choices.x: Help her finish her own habit — gently, with him in the room.
choices.hint: Not an exorcism. A leave-taking. You would be guiding a gentle spirit to set down a task she no longer needs to do, and asking a man to let his wife stop tending him — which may free them both or may be the cruelty he fears.

choices.x: Leave the anchor exactly as it is and teach Kaneda to live beside it.
choices.hint: Cohabitation is a real, documented outcome. But a grief-anchor in a thinning district during Obon is not a fixed thing; what is gentle this week can deepen, and you would be betting his slow hollowing against the membrane holding.

choices.x: Move the anchor — decant the wine into vessels he can actually drink.
choices.hint: A trick more than a rite: split the contact-history across many small cups so the level he must lower is shared, not singular. Clever, and it may simply teach her to fill them all.

beats.scene: Obon, and the door that is open anyway
prose: You do not get to choose the night. It is the thirteenth of August and the lanterns are out along the river and every shrine in Kita has its gate propped for the dead who are, this week and only this week, expected. Whatever you decide to do with Sachiko's bottle, you do it inside that — inside a city that has, for three days, agreed to leave the door open, which is exactly the condition under which a gentle anchor can become something with more reach than it ever wanted. You light the small fire Kaneda's mother would have lit, in the alley, in a chipped dish, because the form matters even to people who say it does not, and Kaneda stands in his own doorway with his hands at his sides like a man at a graveside, which is what this is.

If you choose to help her finish, it does not look like the bureau footage. There is no cold blast, no figure, no voice. There is a bottle that, while you hold the register steady and Kaneda finally says the thing out loud — you can stop now, I've got it, I've got the bar, go on — settles, at last, to two fingers, and does not rise in the morning. If you choose to leave her, the bar simply stays what it has been, a haunted, gentle, slowly emptying man behind a counter, and you carry the knowledge that you let a kindness keep costing him because it was his to spend. Either way you are the one who has to watch his face do the thing faces do when a long argument with the dead is finally, quietly, conceded.

choices.x: Stay until morning, and check the glass with him.
choices.hint: Be present for the result you caused, whatever it is. Witnessing the cost is the least the work asks of you, and the most it can promise.

choices.x: Leave him to the morning alone.
choices.hint: Some leave-takings are not yours to attend. Walking out means trusting a grieving man with his own grief — and never knowing, for certain, which way the level went.

beats.scene: What the honest table pays back
prose: Kaneda is a contact, not a holder and not a node, and the thing he gives you in return is not power or a heading — it is a table you can come back to, which on the roads ahead turns out to be worth more than either. A man who has watched you handle his dead wife with your hands open and your verdict unhidden will, after this, pour you the barley tea and tell you the true thing instead of the safe one, and in a city run on managed information that is a rarer asset than a Tower favour. If you helped Sachiko set down her task, he tells you, the next time you are in, that he slept the whole night through for the first time in six years and hated you for an hour at dawn and then did not. If you left the anchor, he tells you nothing, and pours the tea anyway, and the not-telling is its own kind of trust.

You also carry out a smaller, sharper thing, filed wherever you file the lessons this morning keeps handing you: that the Directorate's neat taxonomy of harm has no column for a love that injures by persisting, and that the gentlest entities in the catalogue are the ones most likely to teach you what you actually believe about letting go. Gin knew this. It is, you are increasingly sure, the exact knowledge the thing wearing him is using against him right now — a duty that injures by persisting, a tending that will not stop because stopping would mean the task is finally over. You leave Kaneda's with the taste of barley tea and the cold understanding that you have just rehearsed, on a bottle of plum wine, the argument you are walking north to have over your brother.

choices.x: Carry the lesson north, toward Gin.
choices.hint: Let the small mercy sharpen the large one. What you learned about a love that injures by persisting is the shape of the thing in Gin — and you go knowing it now, which is worse and better.

choices.x: Mark the table as a place to return.
choices.hint: Bank the trust. An honest counter in Jūjō is a fixed point on roads designed to keep you moving — somewhere the verdict is true and the tea is hot, for after.

sideMissions.title: The Bookseller's Locked Shelf
sideMissions.hook: A shelf behind the counter that no key opens and no fire has ever touched. The books on it have contact-history, and one of them remembers Gin.

beats.scene: A shop that smells of foxed paper and held breath
prose: Sōma's secondhand shop is the kind of narrow that makes you turn sideways between the stacks, three storeys of other people's libraries pressed into a frontage barely wider than its door. The old man has run it since before Gin was born and he does not look up when you come in; he finishes the page he is on, the way booksellers do, asserting that the book outranks the customer. When he does look up he goes very still, and you understand that he has placed you by the face — Gin's jaw, Gin's way of standing in a doorway as if apologising for the space he takes — and that the placing has cost him something. You're the brother, he says, and it is not a question, and behind him, on the high shelf with the small brass lock, something shifts its weight the way a sleeper does when a familiar voice enters the room.

You feel the shelf before you properly see it. It is not loud. It is the opposite of loud — a pocket of held quiet in a shop already quiet, a dozen volumes that have stopped radiating the soft contact-history of handled books and started radiating something denser, more deliberate, the way a word repeated too many times stops being a word. Sōma watches you feel it. Sixty years I've had this shop, he says, and forty of them that shelf has been locked, and I did not lock it. The key turned itself the week your brother stopped coming in.

choices.x: Ask why Gin came in — and what he came in for.
choices.hint: The human thread first. Gin had a reason to frequent a Jūjō secondhand shop, and the reason is on that shelf, and Sōma has been waiting four years for someone with the right face to ask.

choices.x: Read the shelf before you let the old man frame it for you.
choices.hint: Trust your own sight over his telling. Objects with deep contact-history can hold more than memory; reading a locked shelf in a thin district means deciding to know what is on it before you know whether you can put it down.

beats.scene: What objects keep when no one is looking
prose: Sōma makes tea on a hotplate that should have been condemned a decade ago and tells you the part the bureaus would file as folklore and you now know to be field-accurate. Objects are not alive. They do not think. What they have, the old man says — and he says it the way a man says a thing he worked out alone over years and never had anyone to tell — is contact-history: decades of being present when things happened, of being held during specific moments, of sitting in the same room as entities that left a residue the way a fire leaves smoke in cloth. Most books carry a little. A book that was held by the same grieving hands every night for thirty years carries a lot. And a book that was in the room, open, during a crossing — during the exact moment a self came apart at the membrane — carries something that is not memory at all, but a kind of standing wound, a place where the page remembers being a threshold.

That, he tells you, is what the shelf is. Not cursed, which is a word for people who need the comfort of a villain. Accumulated. He bought a dead exorcist's library forty years ago without knowing what some of the volumes had sat through, and the worst of them found their own level on the high shelf the way water finds the low place, and there they have stayed, quietly thickening, a small private membrane of their own behind the counter of a shop in Jūjō. And four years ago your brother came in, white to the lips, and asked to be left alone with the shelf, and the lock — Sōma swears this on his dead wife — turned itself when Gin put his hand flat against the wood.

choices.x: Ask which book Gin held.
choices.hint: Narrow it from a shelf to a single spine. The one Gin reached for is the one that remembers him — and a book that remembers a man can sometimes be made to give him back, in pieces, which is exactly as dangerous as it sounds.

choices.x: Ask what the dead exorcist was, and how he died.
choices.hint: Provenance. A library is its owner's afterlife; knowing what kind of practitioner assembled these volumes tells you what kind of residue you are about to disturb during the one week the door stands open.

beats.scene: The spine that remembers your brother
prose: The lock does for you what it did for Gin: it turns under your hand, the small brass tongue sliding back with a click you feel in your teeth, and the shelf exhales four years of held quiet into the shop. You do not reach blindly. You let your sight walk the spines until one of them looks back — a slim casebound notebook, no title, the boards swollen with damp that was never water — and the moment your attention lands on it you are not in the shop. You are in a low place where the water remembers, and it is night, and a man with your brother's careful hands is writing by lamp-light an argument with himself about whether a debt that was never his to pay might nonetheless be the only honest thing left to do. The book held the room when Gin first found the low place. It kept the threshold. And it has been keeping it, faithfully, on the high shelf, for four years, the way Sachiko's bottle kept filling — an object continuing a function past every reason except the function itself.

This is the find and the danger in one motion. The notebook is a fixed copy of a night you have been trying to reconstruct from the outside — Gin's Saturday, the address in no file, the seam where the entries stop being entries and start being arguments — and to read it is to stand where he stood, in his own dread, at the exact hour the thing wearing him made its reasonable case. It will tell you more than any node ever could. It will also open you, here, in a shop pressed against a private membrane, during the one week the dead are expected, while your unmanaged aperture floods the room with the omnidirectional noise that buried the warning the first time. The book remembers being a threshold. Held by the wrong hands on the wrong night, a threshold is a door, and a door is a thing that opens both ways.

choices.x: Read it here, now, with the shelf open and the city's door propped.
choices.hint: The most Gin you will ever get back, at the highest price. You would be standing in the recorded dread of the night he was turned, in a thinning room, broadcasting — and learning, perhaps, the one thing the nodes could not give you. It will cost your Stability and may cost more.

choices.x: Take it out of the shop sealed, to read somewhere warded.
choices.hint: Patience over hunger. Tanizaki's wards, or the clinic's blue curtain, could let you open the book without opening the room. Slower, safer, and it means carrying a kept threshold through the Obon streets in your own bag.

choices.x: Lock the shelf again and leave the notebook where Gin left it.
choices.hint: The hardest restraint. Gin put his hand flat on this wood and walked away from what it held; there may be a reason he chose to leave the record of his turning sealed, and honouring that means giving up the clearest window you have found.

beats.scene: What it costs to read a kept threshold
prose: Say you read it — most do; you came across a city for exactly this. The notebook does not narrate. It deposits. You get the low place in fragments that arrive in the wrong order, the way Itsuki's sight came back scrambled: the smell of river-mud at slack tide, the particular cold of a place where a great many crossings have happened unmourned, a voice that is not a voice making its case in the register of pure reasonableness — they are owed, and no one will pay them, and you are the only one who can, and is that not the definition of a duty? — and your brother's hand on the page getting tighter and truer with every line until the line between what Gin wanted and what it wanted stops being a line and becomes a rhyme. You learn the address. You learn the shape of the argument. You learn, worst of all, that he was not deceived. He was persuaded, by something that only ever asked him to do what was right, and the persuasion is the most frightening thing you have ever stood inside because you can feel, reading it, how nearly it would work on you.

And the room answers, because you opened the book in it. Sōma's shop goes the particular degree colder that means a residue has noticed a strong unmanaged aperture and oriented toward it; the other spines on the high shelf lean their quiet weight your way; somewhere under the floorboards the building does the listening thing buildings do in this city this week. You do not get out of this clean. Either you spend Stability you cannot spare holding the room shut while you finish reading, or you stop short of the end to keep the membrane from lurching, and never learn the last line your brother wrote before the entries became arguments. Sōma stands by the hotplate with the cold tea going colder and does not interfere, because he is sixty years a bookseller and he has always understood that some books are only honestly read at a price.

choices.x: Finish it — pay the Stability, take the whole night.
choices.hint: The complete record of Gin's turning, and a dent in you that does not buff out. You walk away knowing the address and the argument entire — and a little nearer, yourself, to the omnidirectional noise that is part of the campaign's hidden clock.

choices.x: Stop at the lurch — protect the room, lose the last page.
choices.hint: Choose the district over the data. You keep the membrane from tipping and the shelf from waking the rest of itself, and you carry out an unfinished knowledge that will gnaw at every later road.

beats.scene: The lock, and who keeps it after you
prose: However far you read, the shelf is your problem now in a way it was Sōma's only by accident, and the old man knows it and is, in his dry way, relieved. He has carried a private membrane behind his counter for forty years out of nothing but the bookseller's refusal to burn a book, and he is too old to carry it much longer, and you are the first person to walk in with the right face and the wrong, useful gift. You can re-lock the shelf and leave him the keeping, which means a thinning district has one more quiet wound in it that no bureau will ever survey. You can take the worst of the volumes to Tanizaki, who knows what to do with kept thresholds and will not thank you for the work. Or you can do the thing Gin did not do, and end the notebook — not read it, end it, let the recorded night finally cross the way the man in it never got to — which closes your clearest window forever and may be the only mercy on the shelf.

Whatever you choose, Sōma gives you the one thing a bookseller has to give, which is provenance: the name of the dead exorcist whose library this was, and the fact — offered last, the way the true thing always is — that the man had a student, decades back, who came to nothing the bureaus recorded and may not have come to nothing at all. A thread for later. You leave the shop turning sideways between the stacks the way you came in, the brass lock warm now where a dozen hands have never warmed it, and the street outside doing its Obon business of small fires and propped gates, and you understand that you have added a place to the map your brother drew — a shelf in Jūjō where, if the worst ever comes, a door stands already half-open behind a sixty-year-old counter.

choices.x: Re-lock it and leave Sōma the keeping.
choices.hint: Preserve the window and the wound together. You may need the notebook again; the cost is a thinning district carrying one more sealed threshold and an old man carrying it for you.

choices.x: Take the worst volumes to Tanizaki to be properly warded.
choices.hint: Hand the danger to the one man in Kita who can hold it. It puts you further in Tanizaki's debt and the Grid's orbit — and admits you cannot keep what you found.

choices.x: End the notebook — let Gin's recorded night finally cross.
choices.hint: The mercy that costs you everything the book could still tell. You close your clearest window forever, on purpose, the way Gin closed the lock — and you will never be sure whether you freed something or buried the last of him you could reach.

sideMissions.title: The Grid Courier Gone Dark
sideMissions.hook: A courier who carries between safehouses has missed three drops. The Grid does not call the police; it calls you. Finding her means walking the routes the records cannot see.

sideMissions.title: The Weakening Holder
sideMissions.hook: A domain holder near the thin Kita district is failing. Help him, learn what a seat costs from the inside, or stand in the room when a register lets go and feel the membrane lurch.

sideMissions.title: The Rage That Won't Cool
sideMissions.hook: The Rage seat is under pressure and hard to find on purpose. A holder who has spent decades keeping a furnace banked needs one night's relief, and the cost of giving it.

sideMissions.title: The Fear on the Stairwell
sideMissions.hook: A stairwell in a Kita danchi where the fear is not yours and will not be reasoned with. The Fear holder is too frightened to hold; you are asked to be brave on her behalf.

sideMissions.title: The Hunger With No Address
sideMissions.hook: A holder with no fixed location, moving so the appetite he carries cannot settle. Find him before the campaign-demon's pressure tips the seat — and decide whether a man can be kept from what he holds.

sideMissions.title: The Longing at Shin-Ōkubo
sideMissions.hook: Behind a Korean restaurant, a shrine room where the Longing register draws the homesick in and will not let them leave wanting. A holder under pressure, an Obon crowd, and a door that opens both ways.

sideMissions.title: The Auditor's Anomaly
sideMissions.hook: The bi-monthly assessment cycle has flagged an anomaly that points at Rei. Bury it, explain it, or use it — and learn how the instrument that measures you can be made to lie.

sideMissions.title: Kuroki's Favour
sideMissions.hook: A terrifying ally offers to find what you cannot. The finding is free. The owing is not. A favour from the man who truly runs a stretch of the city is a debt you carry into every later road.

stages.caption: the flirtation that is also a way of never being asked a serious question
scenes: He flirts the way other people change the subject. In the back booth of the place near Ōji that stays open for the men who clean trains, he reaches across and takes the cigarette you are not smoking out of your fingers and puts it behind your ear like a man framing a portrait, and says something light enough to laugh at, and you laugh, and only afterward — walking home under the power lines that hum the way they have hummed all summer over Tokyo — do you understand that he has steered you, gently, expertly, past the one question you came here carrying. It is the oldest move he has. For fifteen years Itsuki has used charm the way the Kuroda use lacquer, a bright skin over the part of the wood that would crack if you touched it directly, and you have always let him, because the alternative was watching him answer honestly and you have never once wanted to be the thing that made him do that.

What you notice — what you have always noticed and filed under later, where you keep the things you cannot afford in a week with a brother in it — is that the lightness costs him. You catch it in the half-second after a joke lands, when his eyes go to the middle distance and something in him counts the door he has just kept shut. He paints overpasses he will not sell and he flirts so that no one will ask why, and you are the only person alive who sees both halves of that arithmetic and says nothing, and the not-saying is its own intimacy, warmer than anything either of you would dare put a name to at this hour, in this booth, with the city humming and your brother gone a Wednesday already.

stages.caption: the real intimacy is that he uses his sight on Gin
scenes: Trust between you was never built out of confessions. It is built out of the cut palm. When Itsuki lays the wet red line along the figure on the bridge and throws his sight through the canvas onto your brother — north, toward water — he is not doing you a favour the way a man does a favour; he is opening the door he has kept shut his whole life and letting you stand in the draught of it. You watch the colour go out of a painting he can never repaint, and you understand that this is the truest thing he has ever said to you: not I love you, which would be a sentence, but here is the part of me the family called lesser, and I am spending it on the person you most need to see. No one has ever trusted you with the thing that wounds them. He hands it over without ceremony, the way he hands you his coat.

And the trust runs the other direction too, which frightens you more. Because he sees Gin and the seated thing layered in the one body, the tide coming in and going out, and he does not look away and he does not soften the reading to spare you — he tells you the seam is closing on a schedule you do not control, in the flat true voice he uses for the overpass paintings, and he trusts you to be able to hear it. You sit on the studio floor in the linseed cold while the colour bleeds out of a bridge he loved, and you realise the intimacy was never going to arrive as a touch. It already arrived, weeks ago, in the willingness of this one man to ruin a beautiful thing rather than let you be alone with what was happening to your family.

stages.caption: after the basin, the night allowed to be ordinary for an hour
stages.gate: you go back to the Nezu compound alone and pay down the name Itsuki was forced to spend — settling his debt to the house with your own measure, unasked, so the thing under the number is no longer owed by him
scenes: The turn is not a confession either. It is what you do while he is asleep on the studio floor. You go back to the Nezu compound alone, before the cleaners, and you put your own measure on the Kuroda ledger in place of the name he spent for you — you settle the debt that was his, the thing under the number, with the only currency a house that old will take, which is yourself. You do not tell him you are going. You let him think you are getting water. It is the first thing in fifteen years you have done for him that he did not steer you away from, because for once you did not give him the chance, and when you come back the dawn is the colour of the inside of a shell and he is awake, sitting up against the wall with the blank canvas turned to face the room, and he knows. Of course he knows. He keeps accounts the way his family does; he felt the number move off his side of it.

He does not thank you, because thanking you would make it a transaction and you have just spent yourself precisely so that it would not be one. Instead he takes you to the row of basins behind the little shrine that has gone quiet this Obon, and he washes the ink and the night off your hands at the third basin the way you wash something you intend to keep, and for one hour the two of you let the morning be ordinary — no seam, no tide, no brother in the north, just water that is only water and a man drying your fingers one at a time on the hem of his paint-stiff shirt. You shouldn't have, he says finally, and it is not a scold, it is the closest he has ever come to the sentence neither of you says. You tell him you know. Neither of you moves to leave. The hour holds, the way a held breath holds, right up until it doesn't.

stages.caption: warmth, unhurried, the rest the night keeps to itself
scenes: You go back to the studio because it is the nearest door and because neither of you can yet stand to be the one who says the day has started. The light comes in low and grey-gold across the canvases leaned three deep against the walls, across the overpass painted and scraped and painted again, and he turns the lamp off rather than on, which tells you everything about which kind of hour this is going to be. He does not perform it and he does not rush it. He has spent his whole life being careful with you; he is careful now, his hand at the side of your face the way it goes to a brushstroke he has finally decided he is allowed to make, and you let yourself, for once, be the beautiful thing he does not scrape back.

What happens after that the night keeps to itself. There is the warmth of him and the linseed cold of the room going slowly warmer, and the city humming on outside the way it has hummed all summer, indifferent and almost kind, and the blank canvas turned to the wall where neither of you can see it. In the morning the colour has not come back to the bridge and it does not matter; some things you spend and do not get back, and lying here unhurried in the grey-gold with his breath gone even against your shoulder, you find you cannot make yourself regret a single thing you have paid out tonight. The north is still there. Gin is still there, faint and frightened and worth all of it. But for this one held hour you are simply a man who is loved, resting, before the road that points toward water asks the rest of you.

stages.caption: the admiration that is also a way of not seeing you
scenes: Nakamura Aoi finds you before you have decided whether to be found. She is a second-year at the Directorate and she carries it like a uniform she is proud of and slightly afraid of creasing, and when she says your brother's name — Gin-san spoke about you, you know — she says it the way people lay flowers, carefully, with both hands. You understand in the first thirty seconds that she has built a Rei already, out of a colleague's offhand affection and two years of wanting the work to mean something, and that the man she has built is taller than you and surer than you and has none of the four sleepless nights currently stacked behind your eyes. It is August in Tokyo and the heat sits on the river like a held breath, and she looks at you across it as though you are the answer to a question she has been too junior to ask aloud.

She noticed the absence before anyone authorised her to. That is the thing you file, the thing that makes you keep talking when the sensible move is to thank her and go: she told you, unprompted, that Gin's disappearance is the wrong shape — not the shape of a man who walked off a caseload, but the shape of a man who was walked. She does not yet know what she has said. She thinks she is offering you comfort, a junior's loyal certainty that her senior would never simply leave. You hear, under the comfort, a person whose instincts are better than her clearance, and you feel the old reflex rise — the one that wants to use what is useful — and you are ashamed of it, and you smile at her anyway, and the smile is the first untrue thing between you.

stages.caption: she is brave for you before she is wise for herself
scenes: Trust arrives, with Aoi, as a risk she takes without telling you the price. She pulls the intake log on Gin's last closed case — the one shut too fast, the address in no file — and she does it from a terminal that keeps her name, because she has decided you deserve to see it and she has not done the arithmetic on what it costs a second-year to be found doing that. When she slides the printout across the table in the noodle place near the Directorate annex, her hand is steady and her voice is not, and you realise she has crossed a line for you that she would never cross for herself, and that this is not strength, exactly — it is something younger and more breakable that has chosen to stand where strength would stand. Shimizu Ren would have her badge for it. She knows. She did it anyway.

So you do the thing you are not used to doing, which is to slow down. You put your hand flat on the printout before you read it and you tell her, plainly, what it could do to her, and you watch her register that you saw the cost when she had hidden it well enough that no one was supposed to. You're the first person who's checked, she says, and looks down, because the hero she built would simply have taken the gift. The tired man across the table did not. That is the moment the shape she carries of you cracks, gently, and the person underneath — smaller, more frightened, more real — turns out to be someone she likes better. You did not want to be loved as Gin's competent shadow. You did not, until now, let yourself notice how much you did not want it.

stages.caption: the turn — gated on standing in front of the fall that was meant for her
scenes: The turn is not a confession; it is the morning the audit lands. Internal Compliance flags the intake pull, and there is exactly one name on the access record, and it is hers, and a second-year does not survive a flag like that — it ends careers quieter and faster than any demon does. You are in the corridor when Shimizu Ren calls her in, and you have a clean way out: it was her query, her clearance, her mistake, and your road through the Directorate stays open if you let the record stand. Instead you walk in first. You tell Shimizu you asked Aoi to run it, that you leaned on a junior's loyalty because you were desperate about your brother, that the lapse is yours to wear. It is mostly true and entirely a choice, and it shuts a door you needed open, and you shut it on purpose, in front of her, so that she will know the difference between being used and being protected.

Afterward she finds you on the annex stairwell where the air-conditioning leaks cold onto the concrete, furious in the particular way of someone who has just been kept safe against her will. I can carry my own mistakes, she says, and you say I know, and you mean it, and that is the whole turn — that you did not save her because she was weak but because you had finally decided her heart was worth more than your road, and you wanted her to outlast this summer whether or not she ever forgave you for it. She is quiet a long time. The river is somewhere below, carrying the first of the Obon lanterns out toward the bay. When she takes your hand it is not gratitude. It is a person choosing, with her eyes open, the man who shut the door — not the one she invented in the spring.

stages.caption: the fade — warm, unhurried, the lanterns going out toward the water
scenes: It is the last night of Obon and the families along the Sumida are setting their dead loose on the current, small lit boats of folded paper that gutter and right themselves and drift, and Aoi stands beside you at the rail with her shoulder against your arm and does not say anything clever, because she has finally stopped needing to be impressive in front of you. You think about Gin out there in the wrong shape, somewhere north, somewhere wet, and you find that for one hour you can hold that grief in one hand and this — her warmth, her breathing, the ridiculous earnest steadiness of her — in the other, and neither cancels the other out. She catches you watching the lanterns and not the water. Come on, she says, gently, and it is the first time anyone has invited you somewhere as though you were allowed to be wanted rather than needed.

Her flat is small and over a shuttered stationer's and smells of the green tea she drinks too much of, and she apologises for the mess that is not a mess, and you understand that the apology is fear wearing manners. So you are careful — careful the way she was brave, which is to say more than is asked. You let the evening be slow. You let her be the one who decides, and she decides, and the city hums its summer hum through the thin glass while the last lanterns reach the dark of the bay and go out one by one. What happens after the light goes off belongs to the two of you and to no file anywhere; in the morning there is the smell of tea again and her hand finding yours before her eyes are even open, and the day with the brother still in it is waiting, and for once you are not facing it alone.

stages.caption: the professional warmth, and the half-second it slips
scenes: You meet Hagiwara Mizuki in the register where everyone meets her: Public Confidence, the smile that has reassured nine hundred frightened civilians that the thing on their landing was a draught and the cold spot a plumbing fault. She is very good. She is the best you have ever watched, and you are a reader by birth and trade, and that is precisely why you notice — the warmth is real the way a stage light is real, exactly as bright as the room requires and not one lumen more, dimmed and raised by a hand you can almost see on the dial. She manages your discomfort about Gin so smoothly that you are halfway to comforted before you catch the technique, and catching it is the first interesting thing that has happened between you, because she watches you catch it, and something behind the performance goes briefly, genuinely still.

It is a half-second and then the smile comes back up and she is once more the woman whose job is the gap between what the public knows and what is happening. But you have read the still place under it now, and you cannot unread it: a discipline thirty years deep, a person who has performed warmth so long and so well that meaning it has become the dangerous, expensive, almost-forgotten thing. You leave the conversation with the file you came for and the small dangerous knowledge that Hagiwara Mizuki noticed you noticing, and did not, for once, reach for the dial.

stages.caption: she gives you what she thinks, not what she says
scenes: Trust with Mizuki is not built out of time spent; she has spent managed time with thousands. It is built out of a single substitution. There comes a night — late, the office emptied, a cover story half-written on her screen about a Kita incident you both know was no plumbing fault — when she stops giving you the public version and gives you, instead, what she actually thinks: that the cover-ups are sometimes the only thing standing between a frightened city and a panic that would get more people killed than the truth ever could, and that she has known this for thirty years and believed it for twenty-nine and has lately, for the first time, begun to lie awake doubting the maths. To say that to anyone is a breach of a discipline she has built her whole self on. To say it to Gin's brother, who reads people for a living and cannot be performed at, is to hand you the one thing she has never given the machine: the cost.

You understand what it is the moment she does it, because you have your own suppressed registers and you know exactly what it takes to let one down on purpose. She is not flirting. She is doing something far more naked than flirting — she is letting a person see the price of the lies she keeps, which she has never let anyone see, because seeing it is the first step to being unable to keep them. The trust runs both ways and frightens you equally: she could end you with a sentence to the right committee, and she is choosing, instead, to be doubted out loud in front of you, which for a woman whose entire value is certainty is the closest thing to undressing she owns.

stages.caption: gated: you protect her breach instead of using it
stages.gate: Rei has to bury or deflect the discrepancy Mizuki let slip — taking a real risk to his own standing to protect her one true thing — rather than trading it to Moriya or the Grid for leverage on Gin.
scenes: The turn is not a confession and it cannot be bought with one. It is gated on what you do with the thing she gave you, because Mizuki has spent thirty years watching people receive a confidence and calculate its market value, and she will not love anyone she has not first watched decline to spend her. The discrepancy she let slip — the doubt, the half-written cover story, the admission that the maths might be wrong — is worth a great deal to the right buyer. Moriya in Internal Affairs would trade you real movement on Gin's file for it. The Grid would take it as proof of what they already believe. You hold, in other words, the exact currency this whole morning has taught you to spend, and the turn happens only if you refuse to spend it — if you take a risk to your own standing to bury her breach, deflect the committee's attention, protect the one true thing she let exist outside the machine, and let her watch you get nothing for it.

When she realises what you have done — and she will realise it, she reads institutions the way you read rooms — the dial-hand comes off the warmth entirely, for the first time since you met her, and what is left is not a performance dimmed to nothing but a woman, tired and thirty years disciplined and astonished to be protected rather than managed. You could have had Gin's file moved, she says, not quite believing it, and you let the silence say that you know, and she crosses the room. What passes between you after that is the thing she has performed a thousand times and meant never: warmth raised by no hand on any dial, exactly as bright as the two of you require and, for once, no one watching to dim it. The door closes on the empty office, and the cover story stays half-written on the dark screen until morning.

stages.caption: one true thing, kept outside the machine
scenes: What you have with Mizuki afterward is not a secret the way her work is a secret; it is the opposite of her work, the one arrangement in her life that no committee manages and no cover story explains. She still performs warmth all day — the city still needs the dial, and she is still the best hand on it the Division has — but she comes back, at night, to the single room where she does not have to, and lets the performance fall off her at the door like a wet coat. You are careful with it the way you are careful with anything that took thirty years to risk. She protects you for real now, which is a more dangerous thing than her job allows, and you protect her breach the way you protected it the first time, and between the two of you there is finally one true thing kept alive outside the machine that you both, in your different ways, serve.

It does not fix what she does for a living and you do not ask it to. Some nights the maths still keeps her awake, and you lie beside her in the dark and do not perform comfort, because she would catch it, and catching it would ruin the only place she has ever been able to stop reading the dial. That is the whole of it and it is enough: the woman whose gift is making frightened people believe the comfortable lie has one person she does not have to lie to, and one room where the warmth she raises is meant. The fade is that room, and the door of it, and the morning that finds the cover story still half-written because for one night neither of you needed it.

stages.caption: the resemblance is the obstacle, not the draw
scenes: Katagiri Noa worked Gin's last months from the inside of the CVD and she knows things about your brother that are not in any file, which is the reason you seek her out and the reason it goes wrong the first three times. She looks at you and flinches — not at you, at the resemblance, the jaw and the doorway-stance and the way you hold a teacup as if apologising to it — and you watch her grief do the arithmetic that grief does, subtracting the living man in front of her from the dead-or-worse one she is mourning, and arriving, every time, at a remainder she cannot stand to sit with. You are, for the first several conversations, not a person to Noa. You are an echo with a pulse, and she is too honest to pretend otherwise and too kind to say it, so she gives you the facts you came for in a voice held very flat and gets you out of her sightline as fast as decency allows.

And you notice her anyway, under the flinch, which is its own complication. You notice that the grief is clean — not the performed grief of the office but the real kind, folded and put away and taken out only when she thinks no one reads her — and that it is grief for a man she clearly loved in some register she has never named even to herself. You notice that she chose not to file something about Gin's last months, kept it back, carried it, which is the act of a person whose loyalties run deeper than her clearance. You notice, in short, a person worth knowing, standing behind a wall built of your own brother's face, and you understand that to be noticed back you will have to become, to her, someone other than the ghost.

stages.caption: she lets a new thing exist without it erasing the old
scenes: Trust arrives the day you stop trying to be a comfort to her about Gin and let her be one to you instead — the day you sit in her grief without managing it, without offering the resemblance as a consolation prize, without doing the thing everyone does and saying he'd be proud in the voice that asks to be thanked. You just let it be true that you are both mourning the same man in different tenses, hers past and yours present, and that neither tense cancels the other. Something in Noa unclenches when she sees that you are not going to use her love for Gin as a door into her, that you would rather she kept it intact than spent any of it on you. She starts, cautiously, to look at you and see you — the tired nineteen-year-old reading every room he enters because he cannot help it, the brother who is not a replacement and has stopped, in front of her, trying to be a balm.

What she gives you in return for not erasing her grief is the thing she chose not to file: the truth of Gin's last months as she watched them from the inside, the changes she logged in her own private memory and never in the system because the system would have done something administrative and irreversible with them. It is a breach of her training and a far deeper trust than the facts themselves — she is telling you that she protected your brother from his own institution, quietly, at risk to herself, out of a love she has never once named. You receive it the way she gave it, without making it about the two of you, and that restraint is what finally lets the wall down. The resemblance stops being a haunting. It becomes, at last, just a family likeness, and she can look at it without subtracting.

stages.caption: gated: you choose her cleanly, not as Gin's echo
stages.gate: Rei has to act on what Noa chose not to file in a way that honours Gin without using Noa as the route to him — and, in a moment where leaning on the resemblance would get him what he wants, deliberately refuse to be the ghost she's grieving.
scenes: The turn is gated on a refusal, and it is the hardest refusal on this road, because the resemblance works and you both know it. There comes a moment — late in the chase north, when you need something only Noa can give and she is raw and the dead man's face is right there on you like a key in a lock — when leaning on the likeness would get you everything: the access, the protection, the closeness, all of it pouring toward you on a current of love that was never meant for you. The turn happens only if you decline to draw on that current.
